Article Title: Trump claims ‘young, beautiful girls’ thank him for making Washington safer
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump highlighted his record on crime and safety during a visit to New York on Friday.

US President Donald Trump on Friday claimed that “young, beautiful girls in the White House” have thanked him for making Washington, DC, safer, as he highlighted his administration’s record on crime during a political event in Long Island, New York.Addressing police officers at the event, held in support of a GOP candidate for governor, Trump repeatedly touted his deployment of the National Guard to cities across the US, including the nation’s capital.“These young, these gorgeous, beautiful girls are -- they want to be safe,” Trump said, without specifying whom he was referring to. He added: “Two years ago, we were in a hellhole, and now we have one of the safest cities.”Trump’s remarks came as the FBI released its 2025 crime statistics. The data showed that the US homicide rate had fallen to its lowest level in 75 years, while overall violent crime declined by 9.3 per cent last year.Trump attributed the improvement to his administration’s law-enforcement measures and National Guard deployment in Washington. However, experts quoted by news agency AP noted that national violent crime rates have been declining since 2022, making it difficult to identify a single cause for the trend.A Council on Criminal Justice report also found that homicides fell 18 per cent nationwide across cities with diverse political leadership.The Long Island event was attended by Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and actor Kelsey Grammer. Blanche and Patel spoke before Trump, with Patel praising the President’s leadership and crediting him for crime reduction.The appearance of senior federal law-enforcement officials at an event supporting Republican candidates also departed from longstanding norms in which law-enforcement agencies generally sought to avoid overtly political gatherings.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump highlighted his record on crime and safety during a visit to New York on Friday. Trump’s remarks came as the FBI released its 2025 crime statistics. The data showed that the US homicide rate had fallen to its lowest level in 75 years, while overall violent crime declined by 9.3 per cent.

The US Army on Friday (local time) announced a temporary halt to all Apache helicopter training missions, two days after a crash in Texas killed both soldiers on board.“The stand-down will remain in effect until we have a better understanding of the root cause of the accident,” the Army said in a statement.The cause of the crash has not been determined, as the investigation is still in its early stages. A safety investigation team from the Army Combat Readiness Center at Fort Rucker, Alabama, is examining the circumstances surrounding the incident.The Army’s statement, however, did not mention any suspension of Apache combat missions currently being carried out in the war in Iran. The helicopters have been operating around the Strait of Hormuz as part of efforts to keep navigation channels open.The military has taken similar measures after previous aviation accidents. Article Title: Michigan shooting: 5 killed, 1 critically injured, suspected gunman found dead after manhunt
Article Text:
This undated poster provided by the Michigan State Police (MSP) Seventh District shows suspect Chad Hickman (Picture credit: AP)

Suspect found dead after manhunt

Police yet to release victims' identities

Five people were killed in a shooting in northern Michigan on Friday, while the suspected gunman was also found dead after a large-scale search, police said.One other person was critically injured and taken to hospital.Michigan State Police said troopers were dispatched at around 11:40 am local time to a home in Missaukee County, about 272 km northwest of Detroit, following a report of a shooting.Officers arriving at the scene found three people dead and a fourth person critically wounded, according to police. The suspect, identified as 39-year-old Chad Hickman, had fled before law enforcement arrived.Police launched an extensive search for Hickman and warned residents that he was armed and dangerous, urging people not to approach him.During the search, investigators discovered a fourth deceased person at another residence, taking the number of victims to five.Police later located Hickman's vehicle in a wooded area near Whitlock Lake. Hickman and another person were subsequently found dead in the area, according to Michigan State Police.Authorities have not disclosed how Hickman or the other person died, and it was not immediately clear whether the additional deceased person found near the vehicle was connected to the shooting.The circumstances surrounding the deaths and the relationship, if any, between the victims and the suspect remain under investigation.“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” Michigan State Police Lieutenant Ashley Miller said in a statement, according to news agency AP.“We remain committed to conducting a thorough investigation and will provide updates as new information becomes available,” she added.Police have not released the names, ages or genders of the victims, saying they were waiting to notify their families.The shooting occurred in Missaukee County, a largely rural area in northern Michigan. Police asked members of the public to avoid the area while investigators continued working at the different locations involved in the case.According to The Guardian, court records show Hickman was in the process of a divorce. The news outlet also reported that he had been sentenced to more than a year in county jail after pleading guilty in 2024 to two misdemeanour charges connected to a 2010 offence.Authorities have not indicated whether those previous cases were connected to Friday's shooting.The investigation remains ongoing, and police have not yet provided a possible motive for the attack.
Article Summary: Suspect Chad Hickman, 39, found dead after large-scale search, police say. Three people dead, one critically injured in shooting in Missaukee County, Michigan. Police yet to release names, ages or genders of victims. Court records show Hickman was in the process of a divorce.

Article Title: A Cape Cod couple moved into their newly built dream home in March 2025; one month later Massachusetts said it would seize it for a new bridge
Article Text:
They Just Built Their Dream Home on Cape Cod—Now the State Will Tear It Down

Hand-delivered notice changes their plans

Aging bridges drive the project

Quick-take law adds to the pressure

Finding another home may be difficult

A Cape Cod couple moved into their newly built dream home in March 2025. Just one month later, Massachusetts officials told them that the state would take the property through eminent domain to make way for a replacement bridge. Marc and Joan Hendel are among 13 property owners in the Round Hill neighborhood of Bourne whose land was selected for the new Sagamore Bridge project. Public records reviewed by the Boston Globe show that by April, the state had taken 11 of the 13 properties. State filings show that Massachusetts had paid at least $4.8 million for six of the homes, more than their combined assessed value of $3.5 million.For the Hendels, however, the money does not make up for the disruption to their retirement plans. After several years living in the Midwest, the couple decided in late 2023 to move to New England to be closer to family in Boston and Connecticut.The couple bought land and signed a contract for a custom-built home in December 2023. They relied on their real estate agent to tell them about any possible problems with the property.Construction finished in early 2025, and the couple moved into the home in March.Four weeks later, a state official arrived with a legal notice saying that Massachusetts was taking ownership of their property.Joan Hendel recalled that they were shocked and did not know how to react. She said that although they have a strong marriage and normally communicate well, they could not find words that day.The Hendels also pointed to documents signed by the seller in 2023 that said the seller was not aware of any planned government taking of the property.State officials had held community meetings about the bridge replacement as early as June 2021. However, the Hendels were living outside Massachusetts at the time and did not know about the local meetings.Massachusetts officials say buying the properties is necessary to improve an important regional transportation route. The Sagamore and Bourne bridges are nearly 90 years old and together handle more than 38 million vehicle trips each year. They are the only road connections between Cape Cod and mainland Massachusetts.Luisa Paiewonsky, executive director of MassDOT's Mega Projects Delivery Office, said that people depend heavily on the bridges.The US Army Corps of Engineers classified the existing bridges as "functionally obsolete" in 2020. Paiewonsky said planners chose a route that would require as few residential property takings as possible.She also acknowledged the impact on residents. Although the state provides compensation for homes and relocation costs and helps people find new housing, she said officials understand that losing a home is much more than a financial transaction. She said the state is working to treat affected residents with respect, professionalism, and compassion because of the disruption the project can cause.Massachusetts is a "quick take" state. This means the government can take legal ownership of a property before the final amount of compensation has been agreed.The case has also raised questions about whether financial payments can truly cover the personal losses caused by forced relocation.A research report by the Pioneer Institute noted that courts have long recognized that a home can have special value to its owner. Losing a property can create emotional pain and moving-related stress that cannot be measured or fully repaid with money.The report also explained that government condemnation powers prevent individual property owners from delaying major infrastructure projects when a particular piece of land is needed.The Hendels face another problem: finding a similar replacement home on Cape Cod.Realtor.com data showed that Barnstable County had 1,402 homes listed for sale in July, with a median price of $946,000. New construction made up only 6.1 percent of the available homes. New homes also cost an average of $654 per square foot, compared with $530 per square foot for older properties.Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, said Cape Cod remains a seller's market because there are not enough homes compared with the number of buyers. He said buyers have few choices and that available homes are expensive. This makes new construction attractive, but also makes the loss of a newly built home especially difficult.Marc Hendel is also worried about the long-term financial effects of having to buy a larger replacement home. He said that if the state provides them with a bigger house, they could face higher property taxes for the rest of their lives. Those extra costs were not part of their retirement plans. He also questioned who would pay for the other unexpected expenses created by the forced move.Joan Hendel had planned to retire within two years. She said those plans are now on hold and described the situation as having seriously disrupted their lives. Along with the 13 homes, Massachusetts plans to acquire three commercial properties in Round Hill so construction of the new bridge can move forward.
Article Summary: Marc and Joan Hendel are among 13 property owners in the Round Hill neighborhood of Bourne whose land was selected for the new Sagamore Bridge project. State filings show that Massachusetts had paid at least $4.8 million for six of the homes, more than their combined assessed value of $3.5 million.

Article Title: A Welsh family lost Menna Owen at 18 after a seizure-triggered cardiac arrest; her heart and lungs were donated to two recipients, both doing well a year later
Article Text:
People in Wales asked to be ‘One in a Million’ as family support for organ donation

Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation Activity Report

Family conversations remove uncertainty

The gap between donors and patients is growing

Deceased organ donors: Increased by 2 percent to 1,428.

Increased by 2 percent to 1,428. Transplants from deceased donors: Increased by 2 percent to 4,666.

Increased by 2 percent to 4,666. Living donors: Increased by 2 percent to 1,017, making up 42 percent of all organ donors.

Increased by 2 percent to 1,017, making up 42 percent of all organ donors. Corneal transplants: Increased by 6 percent.

Overriding donor decisions can cost lives

National report calls for major changes

Increase public consent and donor registrations so they better reflect the strong public support for organ donation.

so they better reflect the strong public support for organ donation. Place Specialist Nurses for Organ Donation within hospital teams to create a stronger culture of organ donation in clinical settings.

to create a stronger culture of organ donation in clinical settings. Improve monitoring and ethical guidance for new and developing transplant practices.

A Welsh family lost 18-year-old Menna Owen after a seizure caused her heart to stop. Her decision to become an organ donor meant that her heart and lungs were given to two young patients, who were both doing very well a year after their surgeries.Menna's story comes as health authorities begin a major campaign to address a sharp fall in family support for organ donation across the United Kingdom.Figures from theby NHS Blood and Transplant show that UK family consent rates fell from 69 percent in 2020/21 to 57 percent in 2025/26. The nearly 20 percent decline comes as the UK transplant waiting list has reached a record 8,296 patients, including 241 children.In response, NHS Blood and Transplant launched the "One in a Million" campaign. It is asking another one million adults to record their donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register (ODR). The aim is to increase registrations from 29 million to 30 million by the beginning of 2027.When Menna suffered a cardiac arrest after an epileptic seizure at her home in Tonteg, Pontypridd, her mother, Beth Owen, already knew what her daughter wanted.Menna was taken by air ambulance to the hospital where Beth works as a Senior Nurse in Neuroscience. After doctors confirmed that Menna had suffered a severe brain injury, Beth spoke to medical staff about organ donation Beth remembered a conversation the family had previously had at home about organ donation. She said Menna had immediately said she wanted to donate everything she could.Menna was described by her mother as kind, quiet, and happy. She loved her dog Ollie, enjoyed reading crime and psychology books, and liked trying new activities. She took part in indoor skydiving and went on the North Wales zip wire. She also wanted to try hang gliding.Menna did not allow epilepsy to stop her from doing the things she enjoyed. She had been looking forward to starting university to study criminal psychology.Because Menna had clearly expressed her wishes, her family did not have to make the difficult decision themselves.Beth said the family had always told Menna and her brother Dan that doing their best was enough. After Menna's death, the family's final act was to respect the decision she had already made about donation.Beth said she was unsure whether the family could have made the same decision without knowing Menna's wishes. Knowing what she wanted made the process much easier.She also said organ donation had brought some comfort to the family during their grief. Knowing that Menna had helped other people and that her wishes had been respected made them feel that she would be proud.A year later, Beth had heard that both recipients were doing extremely well. She described this as part of Menna's lasting legacy.Official figures show that family support for donation is around 90 percent when a person's decision is recorded on the ODR. However, consent falls below 50 percent when families do not know what their loved one wanted.In Wales, 1.4 million people have registered their donation decision. The number of deceased organ donors increased from 115 to 126 over the past year, but the number of transplants received by Welsh residents fell slightly from 235 to 224.There are currently 348 patients in Wales on the active transplant waiting list.Across the UK, figures for 2025/26 show similar pressure:Despite these increases, 434 people across the UK died while waiting for a transplant last year, including 16 people in Wales. Another 899 people were removed from waiting lists because their health became too poor for transplantation.NHS Blood and Transplant officials warned that families can sometimes go against a recorded donation decision when they are faced with end-of-life decisions without enough preparation.Anthony Clarkson, Director of Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation at NHS Blood and Transplant, said family support for donation has been falling steadily in recent years and needs to improve.He said the "One in a Million" campaign is asking people in Wales to register their donation decisions and help increase the number of people on the NHS Organ Donor Register to 30 million by the beginning of 2027.Having a recorded decision gives families certainty about what their loved one wanted and makes it more likely that the decision will be respected.Clarkson also warned that some families still reject organ donation even when their loved one had clearly wanted to donate. This results in hundreds of possible transplant opportunities being lost every year.He urged people who have not yet recorded their wishes to join the Organ Donor Register and encouraged families to remember and respect those decisions.The long-term pressure on transplant waiting lists has also led to calls for wider changes across the healthcare system.The Organ Donation Joint Working Group (ODJWG) published a report calling for a "bolder, braver approach to organ donation." The report followed figures showing that nearly 5,000 people in the UK had died while waiting for a transplant over the previous decade.The ODJWG identified three main goals:Menna's story shows why knowing a person's wishes can matter so much. Her family did not have to make an impossible decision during a time of grief because Menna had already made it herself. Her heart and lungs went on to help two young people, giving her family a lasting source of comfort and a powerful legacy.
Article Summary: Welsh family lost 18-year-old Menna Owen after a seizure caused her heart to stop. Her decision to become an organ donor meant that her heart and lungs were given to two young patients. NHS Blood and Transplant launched the "One in a Million" campaign. It is asking another one million adults to record their donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register.

Article Title: Europe is racing to eradicate a crayfish that can reproduce without mating; in the Czech Republic, two newly detected populations are being targeted before they spread
Article Text:
Conservationists in Europe are racing to stop the next invasive species before it spreads

Fast funding targets small populations

Experts say prevention is better than control

Projects target many invasive species

Other projects include:

Removing common myna populations through the National Research Council of Italy (CNR-IRET).

Eradicating red-billed leiothrix from coastal dune habitats in Flanders through INBO.

Protecting the native Cretan wall lizard from invasive Italian wall lizards through the University of Crete.

Removing Japanese knotweed from Austria's Dürrenstein-Lassingtal Wilderness Area.

Controlling Turkish warrantcabbage in species-rich grasslands on Italy's Asiago Plateau.

Removing invasive Ludwigia and alligator weed from Portuguese rivers through the Comunidade Intermunicipal da Região de Coimbra.

Local communities are also helping

European conservationists have started targeted eradication efforts against newly discovered populations of self-cloning marbled crayfish in the Czech Republic. They are trying to remove the species before it can spread through local waterways.The work in Moravia is part of a wider European Union effort to stop invasive alien species while their populations are still small enough to remove completely.The Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic is leading the local project, which targets two newly discovered groups of marbled crayfish. Unlike almost all other freshwater crustaceans, marbled crayfish reproduce through parthenogenesis. This means a single female can produce genetically identical offspring without mating.The species can therefore increase its numbers quickly. It also carries crayfish plague, a fungal disease that has badly reduced native European crayfish populations.The Czech project is among the first 20 projects supported by the European Invasive Alien Species Rapid-Response Fund. Co-funded by the European Union and carried out through IUCN Save Our Species, the fund provides grants of €10,000 to €50,000.The money allows government agencies, research institutes, and conservation groups to act quickly when new invasive species are discovered.The European Environment Agency (EEA) said in a briefing published in June 2026 that although the EU is making progress against biological invasions, non-native species continue to spread into new areas.The report stressed that finding invasive species early and removing them quickly is one of the best ways to prevent long-term environmental damage.Across Europe, non-native species are estimated to cause about USD 28 billion in environmental damage, lost economic activity, and management costs every year. Worldwide, invasive alien species have contributed to 60 percent of recorded animal and plant extinctions and were the only recorded cause in 16 percent of those cases.In the past, much conservation funding has focused on controlling invasive species after they become widespread. At that stage, removing them can be extremely difficult, expensive, or impossible.Professor Helen Roy, Co-Chair of the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group, explained why early action is important. Every invasive species that becomes a major problem started as a small population somewhere. Removing new populations while they are still limited to small areas gives conservationists a much better chance of preventing damage that could last for decades.The Convention on Biological Diversity also published a practical toolkit in 2025 to help countries meet Target 6 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Developed with IUCN specialists, the guidance explains how governments can create monitoring systems and rapid eradication plans.The first round of funding supports projects in nine European countries. The projects cover marine, freshwater, forest, and urban environments.In Croatia, the Hippocampus Association for Environmental Protection is using divers and marine scientists to remove venomous lionfish from protected areas in the Adriatic Sea before they damage native fish populations.In Belgium, the Province of Antwerp, the Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO), and other authorities are using environmental DNA (eDNA) testing and targeted traps to remove isolated populations of American bullfrogs and African clawed frogs from wetlands in Flanders and Wallonia.Some projects also involve cooperation across national borders. National Park Thayatal in Austria and Podyjí National Park in the Czech Republic are working together to remove non-native raccoons. The effort aims to protect ground-nesting birds and native European wildcats.In the Czech Republic, the Czech Society for Ornithology is removing the Oriental turtle dove from its only known non-native breeding site in Europe.In Finland, local residents are taking part directly in invasive-species monitoring. People in Vantaa are using a mobile app to record and confirm the manual removal of Himalayan balsam along the Mätäoja urban stream.Technical support for these projects comes from the global network of the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group. Lessons from the first 20 projects will also help shape IUCN's wider Invasive Alien Species Strategy.The European Invasive Alien Species Rapid-Response Fund will accept more applications until 10 February 2027, or until its available funding runs out. Conservation groups and research organisations across the EU are being encouraged to apply by September 2026 so they can respond to new invasive species before the populations become permanently established.
Article Summary: The European Invasive Alien Species Rapid-Response Fund provides grants of €10,000 to €50,000. The money allows government agencies, research institutes, and conservation groups to act quickly when new invasive species are discovered. The first round of funding supports projects in nine European countries.

Article Title: Berlin Volksbuhne swimming pool’s ‘Black people only’ event faces backlash, gets cancelled over security concerns amid racism and inclusion debate
Article Text:
Berlin swimming pool cancels ‘Black communities only’ event over security concerns after backlash (Photo: AFP)

Why was the Black-community swimming event cancelled?

What is the Berlin pop-up swimming pool?

Why is the pool project controversial?

What is Each One Teach One?

Berlin pool controversy comes amid separate German swimming row

Lifeguard says language barrier created safety concerns

AfD enters the swimming pool controversy

Volksbuhne is one of Berlin’s historic theatres

A temporary public swimming pool outside Berlin’s historic Volksbuhne theatre has cancelled a planned event that was due to be open exclusively to Black communities after the programme attracted controversy and scrutiny over its restricted access. The €300,000 pop-up pool, which opened last week as an eight-week summer facility, had planned to close its 25-metre pool to the general public from 12pm to 6pm on Friday, August 14, for an event organised in partnership with anti-discrimination community project Each One Teach One (EOTO).The Volksbuhne website had described the session as being “open exclusively to Black communities”, with visitors asked to respect the collective self-designation and the space associated with it. The theatre has since cancelled the event, citing security concerns and saying that swimming activities involving Black children and teenagers had become targets of right-wing and racist harassment.The decision has triggered a wider debate in Germany over inclusion, public funding and access to public spaces. The temporary pool was originally presented as a symbol against exclusion and commercialisation and as a free summer meeting place for Berlin residents.It is funded by the Volksbuhne, which receives more than €20 million in public funding annually, while the pop-up pool itself has a reported budget of around €300,000 and is expected to attract approximately 20,000 visitors during its eight-week run. The facility can accommodate 46 swimmers at a time. While organisers described the planned Black-community event as an effort to create a safer and more inclusive environment, critics questioned why a publicly funded facility would restrict access to the majority of residents for several hours.The Volksbuhne said the decision to cancel the event was based on security concerns.According to the theatre, the cancellation followed concerns that swimming opportunities for Black children and teenagers had increasingly become targets of right-wing and racist harassment.The event was being organised in collaboration with EOTO, a publicly funded organisation that runs social and cultural programmes for Black communities.The theatre’s original announcement said that on August 14, the pool would be closed to the general public between noon and 6pm and reserved exclusively for Black communities.The wording prompted criticism from people who questioned whether an event at a publicly funded facility should exclude other members of the public.The temporary outdoor swimming pool was installed in front of the Volksbuhne am Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz in Berlin and officially opened last week.The facility is expected to remain in operation for eight weeks and was promoted as a free summer gathering place for local residents.The pool is 25 metres long and can accommodate up to 46 swimmers at any one time. Organisers estimate that around 20,000 people could use it during its temporary run.The project has been described as an attempt to provide more opportunities for swimming in Berlin at a time when many existing pools are unavailable.Volksbuhne director Matthias Lilienthal defended the broader idea behind the temporary facility in an interview with German broadcaster ZDF.“Half of the indoor and outdoor pools are closed, so we thought we’d help out Governing Mayor Kai Wegner,” he said.Lilienthal also described the project through the theatre’s artistic lens, saying the Volksbuhne considers even something as ordinary as two people splashing each other to be a theatrical event.The controversy centres partly on the fact that the pool is publicly funded and was promoted as an inclusive community space.The Volksbuhne receives more than €20 million in public funding every year, while the temporary swimming project itself reportedly costs approximately €300,000.The facility is free for visitors, meaning members of the public do not have to pay to use it.The planned six-hour event for Black communities was therefore criticised by some Berlin residents who felt they would be excluded from a publicly funded facility.Organisers, however, framed the event differently, arguing that creating a dedicated space for Black communities was connected to concerns about racism and harassment.The cancellation means the proposed event will no longer take place, although the temporary pool itself is expected to continue operating as planned.Each One Teach One, known as EOTO, is a community organisation focused on Black people in Germany and works on social, educational and cultural programmes.It was the partner for the planned swimming event at the Volksbuhne.The organisation’s involvement reflected the stated aim of creating a dedicated space for Black communities, particularly amid concerns about discrimination and harassment.The controversy has nevertheless raised questions about how publicly supported cultural institutions should balance targeted community programmes with universal access to public facilities.The dispute in Berlin comes shortly after another controversy involving swimming in Germany.At the Heidebad lakeside beach in Halle, eastern Germany, a lifeguard introduced a controversial policy requiring bathers to understand German safety instructions or risk being prevented from swimming.Lifeguard Mathias Nobel said the measure was motivated by safety concerns after he had reportedly rescued a toddler who nearly drowned after entering a section of the lake that reaches approximately 138 feet in depth.Nobel said he had struggled to communicate safety instructions to some families who did not speak German.The policy was quickly labelled a “German-only” rule and attracted accusations of discrimination and racism. Authorities in Halle subsequently told him to reverse the language restrictions and warned that measures that could be perceived as xenophobic could damage the city’s reputation.Nobel has denied accusations of racism and maintained that the issue was about safety, communication and respect for lifeguards.Nobel said that some families could not understand him when he attempted to explain safety rules.He told The Telegraph that he had encountered situations where parents appeared unable to understand questions about their children’s ages or safety equipment.He argued that a language barrier could potentially have serious consequences at a swimming location where lifeguards need to communicate quickly during emergencies.However, the German life-saving association criticised the approach, while the country’s anti-discrimination agency noted that there are no equivalent requirements imposed on German tourists when they swim abroad.The Halle dispute also became part of Germany’s broader political debate over immigration.The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) seized on the controversy, claiming that swimming pools were becoming “danger zones” and arguing that authorities were losing control over public safety.The issue has emerged as immigration remains a major political topic in Germany, particularly ahead of elections in Saxony-Anhalt.The centre-right Christian Democratic Union is currently the largest party in the state parliament, while the AfD finished second in the previous election and holds 23 of the legislature’s 83 seats.At the national level, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government has also adopted a tougher position on immigration amid pressure from the AfD.The Volksbuhne am Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz dates back to 1914 and is regarded as one of Berlin’s most historic theatres.It attracts approximately 130,000 visitors and stages an average of around 20 events each week.The temporary swimming pool represents an unusual extension of the institution’s cultural programming, with the theatre describing the project as both a public service and an artistic intervention.The cancellation of the Black-community event has now placed the project at the centre of a much wider conversation about racism, inclusion, public funding and who should have access to publicly supported spaces.
Article Summary: Pop-up pool opened in front of Berlin's historic Volksbuhne theatre last week. Event was planned to be open exclusively to Black communities on August 14. The venue has since cancelled the event, citing security concerns. The decision has triggered a wider debate in Germany over inclusion and access.

Article Title: Why Putin’s first Kuril Islands visit matters as Russia-Japan ties hit new low
Article Text:
File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin watches a military exercise from the board of the Varyag missile cruiser of the Pacific Fleet near Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on Sakhalin Island, Russia

Putin visits Iturup, inspects local industry

Why the Kuril Islands are disputed

Japan protests Putin's visit

Ukraine war deepens Russia-Japan tensions

Visit comes amid wider military tensions in the region

Ukraine battlefield developments add to regional backdrop

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way for countries to resolve long-standing territorial disputes? Bilateral diplomatic negotiations Binding international legal arbitration 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

No breakthrough in decades-old territorial dispute

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the disputed Kuril Islands for the first time, travelling to Iturup as Moscow's relations with Japan remain deeply strained over Russia's war in Ukraine.The visit, reported by Russian state media on Thursday, comes after Putin oversaw military exercises involving Russia's Pacific Fleet in the country's Far East.It also comes a day after North Korea, a close Russian ally, fired a ballistic missile towards waters off the Korean Peninsula.Putin's trip to Iturup is significant because the island is among four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory and calls the Northern Territories.According to Reuters, Putin visited the Yasny fish-processing plant on Iturup and was shown local fishing operations. Russian television footage showed him examining large tuna and halibut and sampling fish roe.The Russian president also interacted with residents."What lovely weather you have there, just like a resort!" Putin told a group of locals.The visit followed Putin's inspection of the Pacific Fleet's flagship missile cruiser Varyag during military exercises in Russia's Far East.Russian state news agency TASS described the Iturup trip as Putin's first personal visit to the Kuril island chain.Putin had previously visited Sakhalin but had not personally travelled to the disputed islands.The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the Kuril Islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945.The four islands at the centre of the dispute are Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets. Japan refers to them as Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai Islands and maintains that they are Japanese territory.The Soviet Union retained control of the islands after the war, and Russia has maintained a military presence there.The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and northern Japan. They also have rich fishing grounds and deposits of minerals, including gold and silver.Around 20,000 people currently live on the islands under Russian administration, while Japan says its former residents were displaced following the Soviet takeover. Around 17,000 Japanese residents were deported after the islands were occupied in 1945.Putin's visit has drawn a strong reaction from Tokyo.Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi protested the visit, reiterating Japan's claim over the islands."The northern territories, including Etorofu, are Japan's inherent territory both historically and based on international law," Motegi said, according to Reuters."Japan strongly protests this visit."The territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty formally ending their World War II conflict.There have been several attempts to resolve the dispute over the decades. In 1956, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested that two of the disputed islands could be returned to Japan as part of a peace settlement, although no final agreement followed.Negotiations resumed after the collapse of the Soviet Union, but the territorial dispute remained unresolved.The long-running dispute has become more difficult to resolve since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Japan joined Western countries in imposing sanctions on Moscow and has strongly supported Ukraine. In response, Russia suspended peace treaty negotiations with Japan and halted several forms of economic cooperation relating to the disputed islands.Moscow has also accused Tokyo of adopting an increasingly hostile position towards Russia.Putin used his address to Pacific Fleet personnel on Wednesday to criticise Japan's sanctions and its continuing territorial claims. He said Russia had previously maintained constructive relations with Tokyo over the issue during the administration of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, but claimed Japan had since changed its position.He noted that Japan's current territorial claims came despite what he described as the post-World War II territorial arrangements being reflected in international documents.Putin also recalled the 1956 Soviet-Japanese declaration, which restored diplomatic relations and opened the way towards a possible peace treaty and a settlement of the island dispute. He claimed that Tokyo later refused to abide by the declaration.Russia has increasingly strengthened its military presence and activities in its Far Eastern territories as tensions with Japan have risen.Putin's Kuril Islands trip also comes against a backdrop of increased military activity in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president had travelled to the Far East to oversee the final stage of large-scale Pacific Fleet exercises, which began on August 4.Putin said the exercises were necessary to maintain military readiness and protect Russia's interests and security in the Asia-Pacific region. He also accused NATO of seeking to increase its presence in the region.Putin warned of rising conflict potential in the Asia-Pacific and Arctic regions, while criticising what he described as plans to deploy new weapons systems in the region.The timing was notable because North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday, just days before major South Korea-US military exercises are scheduled to begin. Moscow and Pyongyang have significantly deepened their military partnership in recent years.Putin's visit comes as Russia's war in Ukraine continues with fighting and long-range strikes intensifying.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had recaptured about 745 sq km of territory this year across parts of the southeastern front, including 26 settlements in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. However, these battlefield claims have not been independently verified.Ukraine has also stepped up attacks deep inside Russian territory, including a major recent strike on Novorossiysk, a key Black Sea port and grain-export hub.The attack reportedly damaged port infrastructure and disrupted operations at major grain terminals.Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, making Novorossiysk strategically important not only for Moscow but also for global agricultural markets.At the same time, Russia has continued missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.For Japan, Putin's visit is likely to further complicate already strained relations with Moscow.The Kuril Islands remain one of the most enduring territorial disputes left over from World War II.While there have been periods of diplomatic engagement and economic cooperation, neither side has been able to agree on a final settlement.With Russia's war in Ukraine having pushed Moscow and Tokyo further apart, Putin's first personal visit to the disputed islands sends a strong political signal that Russia has no immediate intention of softening its position over territory it has controlled since 1945.
Article Summary: Putin visited Iturup, one of the four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory. The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and Japan.

Article Title: Zelenskyy seeks 10% of US stockpile to 'destroy all Russians’ missiles’: Report
Article Text:
Zelensky urged the US to sell Ukraine 5-10% of its Patriot interceptor stockpile to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks

Zelensky describes daily efforts to secure missiles

Uncertainty over Ukraine's Patriot production

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of the US providing more Patriot missiles to Ukraine? Yes, absolutely No, they should focus on diplomacy 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zelensky seeks greater US role in peace talks

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.Zelensky made the comments in an interview with CNN as Ukraine faces a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile attacks and a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors.“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025,” he said. “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.”“If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%.”Zelensky said Russia's intensified attacks had placed further pressure on Ukraine's air defences, particularly around Kyiv. The United Nations has said July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022.“Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”Zelensky said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority, involving direct appeals to the US and negotiations with other allies.“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it.”He said the global supply of Patriot missiles had been strained by the US war with Iran, during which American and Gulf forces used dozens of interceptors against Iranian missile and drone attacks.The shortage has left Ukraine facing growing difficulty in defending its cities against Russian missile strikes.Zelensky also said uncertainty remained over a proposal for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles under a US licence.US President Donald Trump had said during the Nato summit in Ankara that he would allow Ukraine to obtain a licence to manufacture the systems. However, Trump later expressed uncertainty about the proposal.Patriot system manufacturers have since sent officials to Kyiv to discuss potential production, but Zelensky said no agreement had yet been reached.“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”Zelensky said he had been appealing directly to the White House through calls and messages, as well as through Ukraine's allies, to secure additional Patriot support.Zelensky also said Ukraine had presented new proposals for the US-led peace process, while calling for greater American involvement.“We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan. I’m thankful to the team of President Trump that they want to continue. (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn’t want to stop this war now and (there’s) not enough pressure on him now.”He rejected the possibility of Ukraine surrendering the remaining territory in the Donbass sought by Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying security guarantees remained essential to prevent another invasion.“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?”Zelensky also backed Western assessments that Putin could eventually seek to escalate the conflict with Nato, including by targeting the Baltic states.“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in Nato or not in Nato. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles. He said even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelenski said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority.
