Article Title: Indian-origin teen charged with murdering mother, brother in US after ‘kill family’ searches
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

A 17-year-old Indian-origin teenager has been charged with allegedly murdering his mother and younger brother at their home in Acton, Massachusetts, authorities said.The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery on a household or family member and assault and battery, along with charges of using a vehicle without authority and stealing a motor vehicle.The 17-year old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, inside their Martha Lane home on Tuesday before fleeing in his mother's car.Middlesex district attorney Marian Ryan and acton police chief Douglas Sturniolo said police received a call from teen's father shortly after 6.37 pm on August 11 after he was unable to contact his family. A tutor expected at the house had also been unable to reach anyone.The father had last spoken to Sudha early Tuesday morning before leaving for work, while Siddharth was last seen around noon, authorities said.Police who arrived at the house found both victims dead. Siddharth was found on the first floor and Sudha in the finished basement. Both victims were found with “obvious trauma”, but the chief medical examiner has yet to release information on the exact cause and manner of death.The type of weapon used in the killings is also still under investigation.The accused was not at the house when police arrived and was believed to have fled in his mother's vehicle. Investigators issued an alert for him as they searched for the teenager.He was found early Wednesday in the vehicle in a parking lot in Wayland, Massachusetts, after local police responded to an unrelated alarm. He was taken into custody without incident.The Middlesex county district attorney's office said investigators found that Arjun had recently displayed concerning behaviour."The subsequent investigation indicates that Arjun had recently been demonstrating concerning behaviour, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasies regarding killing his family,” the statement said.Arjun was expected to be arraigned in Lowell juvenile court on Wednesday. However, the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over murder charges. He will therefore face arraignment on the murder and related assault charges in Concord district court later.
Article Summary: Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts. The 17-year-old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14. The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually…" - a lesson on stepping outside your comfort zone
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

"When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that"

Where this quote actually comes from

What the quote is actually saying

Why discomfort can genuinely be a sign of progress

Why stepping outside a comfort zone actually matters

Why failure is genuinely part of growth

Why real confidence tends to develop through experience, not before it

Why this idea applies directly to professional life

A note on Melinda French Gates

Other famous quotes by Melinda French Gates

"That is why we women have to lift each other up, not to replace men at the top of the hierarchy, but to become partners with men in ending hierarchy."

"I've never held the view that women are better than men, or that the best way to improve the world is for women to gain more power than men."

"Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it."

"I am simply not willing to accept that my granddaughters could grow up with less freedom than I did."

Why this quote continues to inspire people

Growth rarely feels comfortable while it is actually happening. Learning something new, taking on more responsibility, or simply stepping into an unfamiliar situation tends to bring real uncertainty along with it. Melinda French Gates put a name to that discomfort directly. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that," she said. Rather than treating discomfort as an automatic warning sign, her point is that it often means something else entirely, that an old habit or a familiar limit is genuinely being challenged, and that the challenge itself is usually exactly where real growth actually happens. Her words encourage people to look at discomfort with greater curiosity, recognising that difficult moments can sometimes signal progress rather than failure or a reason to retreat. That practice of consciously reframing discomfort as evidence of growth, rather than a signal to retreat, reflects a deliberate mental habit French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day, released the same year. She went further in the same conversation, describing exactly how she talks herself through discomfort in real time. "I'll literally coach myself in my head," she said. "'Okay, this is hard, but I must be growing here. It's going to be okay.' And then on the other side, you actually become far more resilient. " She added a piece of broader advice in the same interview too, "Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it... just know you've got a lot of tools inside of you." For French Gates, that mindset reflects the value of recognising difficult moments as opportunities to adapt, learn and develop greater confidence.Staying inside a comfort zone usually means staying inside the familiar, where there is less uncertainty and fewer situations that genuinely test existing ability. Growth tends to happen specifically once someone runs into something unfamiliar instead, a new responsibility that feels overwhelming, a moment of speaking up that feels intimidating, a new skill that feels frustrating at first. None of that discomfort is pleasant in the moment. It is often exactly what gradually expands what a person is actually capable of. This is why people who consistently seek out unfamiliar challenges tend to develop broader skill sets over time, while those who remain within familiar routines, however comfortable, often find their growth quietly stalling without ever fully realising it.Comfort usually comes from familiarity. When something feels uncomfortable, it often simply means someone has not fully mastered it yet, and that unfamiliarity is precisely what creates room to actually learn. A first attempt at something new is rarely smooth. Repeated effort is usually what eventually turns that uncertainty into real confidence, which is really how most skills get built in the first place.Comfort zones are not inherently a problem. They provide genuine stability and give people room to recover between challenges. The real issue starts once fear of discomfort stops someone trying anything new at all. Taking calculated steps beyond a familiar routine tends to expose people to new ideas and real opportunity, and over time, the boundaries of what actually feels comfortable start expanding on their own.Growth does not only happen through success. A mistake can reveal exactly where a real weakness sits. A difficult conversation can improve how someone communicates going forward. A rejected opportunity can push someone to prepare more thoroughly next time. Rather than treating every setback as proof of inadequacy, it can just as easily become useful information that helps someone actually improve.Confidence is not always something someone has to already possess before taking action. More often, it develops precisely because they took the action despite feeling genuinely uncertain about it. Each difficult experience becomes real evidence that a person can actually handle a challenge, and that evidence is what slowly builds resilience and self-belief over time.Career growth regularly requires people to take on responsibilities they have never handled before. A promotion might suddenly demand real leadership skill. A new job might involve completely unfamiliar systems. Avoiding those moments can feel comfortable in the short term, but it tends to limit development considerably further down the line, while embracing a reasonable challenge tends to open the door to real professional growth instead.Melinda French Gates is an American philanthropist, author and advocate who has worked extensively on global health, gender equality and women's economic empowerment. She co-founded the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, stepped away from it in 2024, and went on to lead Pivotal Ventures, an investment and incubation organisation she founded to advance social progress. Her 2019 book The Moment of Lift: How Empowering Women Changes the World explored many of these same themes at length.French Gates' words offer a genuinely simple way to rethink the moments that actually make people uncomfortable. Not every difficult experience is really a setback. Sometimes discomfort is exactly the evidence that someone is learning, adapting and becoming capable of something they genuinely could not do before. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" is really a reminder to approach unfamiliar experiences with curiosity rather than retreating from them immediately. Growth takes real patience, involves real mistakes, and often just requires the courage to stay in an uncomfortable situation long enough to actually learn something from it.
Article Summary: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" Melinda French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day. French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.

Article Title: Where is Bashar al-Assad? Ousted Syrian dictator sentenced to death in absentia
Article Text:
Synrian Ex-president Bashar Assad (2019 photo)

where is Bashar al-Assad now, and can Syria ever bring him back to face the punishment handed down by its court?

Assad remains in Russia after fleeing Syria

Where exactly in Moscow is Assad living?

Bashar Assad, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during their meeting in Moscow, Russia.

Russia has kept Assad away from public life

Why Syria sentenced Assad to death

Syria sentences absent Bashar al-Assad to death over killings and torture (Image: Reuters)

Verdict welcomed by Assad's victims

Can Syria actually bring Assad back?

From Syria's president to a secluded exile

Bashar al-Assad inherited his presidency from his father

A Syrian criminal court in Damascus has sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia after finding him guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year civil war. The verdict, delivered on Tuesday, August 11, marks the first conviction against Assad by Syria's transitional authorities since his regime collapsed in December 2024. But while the court has pronounced a death sentence, the former Syrian ruler remains far beyond the reach of the authorities who now control Damascus.Assad is currently in Russia, where he and his family were granted asylum after fleeing Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. His precise location inside Russia has not been publicly confirmed. However, reporting over the past year has placed the former dictator in Moscow, with sources previously indicating that his family was likely living in the heavily guarded Rublyovka area, an affluent district on the western outskirts of the Russian capital.The death sentence therefore raises a central question:The most recent credible reports continue to place Assad in Moscow.Reuters reported after Tuesday's verdict that Assad "is currently in Russia", where he and his family received asylum on humanitarian grounds. His brother Maher al-Assad, who also received a death sentence in absentia, is likewise believed to be in Russia.Assad's escape from Syria came on December 8, 2024, when rebel forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa swept into Damascus after a lightning offensive that lasted less than two weeks. The advance brought down the Assad government and ended more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.At the time, Assad's whereabouts were initially unknown. Russia's foreign ministry said he had resigned and left Syria, while reports suggested he had travelled from the coastal region before being flown to Russia. Russian state media subsequently reported that Assad and his family had arrived in Moscow and had been granted asylum.In a statement issued after his escape, Assad disputed accounts that he had planned his departure in advance. He said he had remained in Damascus until the final hours and later moved to a Russian military base in Latakia as the security situation deteriorated."First, my departure from Syria was neither planned nor did it occur during the final hours of the battles, as some have claimed," Assad said in the statement."On the contrary, I remained in Damascus, carrying out my duties until the early hours of Sunday, December 8, 2024," he added.According to Assad's account, he travelled to the Russian Khmeimim airbase in Latakia after opposition forces entered Damascus and intended to continue overseeing military operations. He said the situation at the base then became untenable and Moscow asked its command to arrange his evacuation."With no viable means of leaving the base, Moscow requested that the base's command arrange an immediate evacuation to Russia on the evening of Sunday 8 December," the statement said.Independent reporting has also described Assad's departure as a Russian-assisted evacuation. The Guardian reported in December 2025 that Assad and his sons were taken under Russian military escort to Khmeimim before being flown out of Syria.This is where the trail becomes less certain. There is no publicly verified address for Assad in Moscow, and he has rarely, if ever, been seen publicly since arriving in Russia. A detailed Guardian investigation published in December 2025, based on sources in Russia and Syria, a family friend and leaked data, reported that the Assad family was likely living in Rublyovka, a prestigious gated area associated with Russia's political and business elite.The report described the family's life in Moscow as secluded and closely controlled. A family friend said Assad had little contact with the outside world and remained in touch with only a small number of people who had served around his presidential palace."It's a very quiet life," said the family friend. "He has very little, if any, contact with the outside world. He's only in touch with a couple of people who were in his palace, like Mansour Azzam [former Syrian minister of presidency affairs] and Yassar Ibrahim [Assad's top economic crony]."The same investigation said Assad was studying Russian and revisiting his training in ophthalmology. Before entering politics, Assad had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and had originally intended to pursue a medical career before the death of his elder brother Basil changed the succession plans of the Assad family."He’s studying Russian and brushing up on his ophthalmology again," a family friend told the Guardian. "It’s a passion of his, he obviously doesn’t need the money. Even before the war in Syria began, he used to regularly practice his ophthalmology in Damascus."However, the Rublyovka location should be treated as a reported possibility rather than a confirmed current address. What is firmly established is that Assad remains in Russia and has been kept away from public political life.Moscow's decision to shelter Assad has been one of the biggest obstacles to attempts by Syria's new authorities to bring the former president before a court.Russia granted Assad and his family asylum on humanitarian grounds after the fall of his government. Since then, reports have indicated that the Kremlin has placed restrictions on his public activities.In a November 2025 interview cited by the Guardian, Russia's ambassador to Iraq, Elbrus Kutrashev, said Assad was safe in Russia but could not engage in political or media activity."Assad may live here but cannot engage in political activities … He has no right to engage in any media or political activity. Have you heard anything from him? You haven’t, because he is not allowed to – but he is safe and alive," Kutrashev said.The restrictions have contributed to the mystery surrounding Assad's life in exile. Unlike other deposed leaders who have appeared publicly after leaving office, Assad has remained largely invisible.His children, however, have had a somewhat more visible life in Moscow. The Guardian reported that Assad's daughter Zein attended the prestigious Moscow State Institute of International Relations, known as MGIMO, and graduated in June 2025. Other family members were also seen at the ceremony, although they kept a low profile.The family has also reportedly travelled to the United Arab Emirates, a destination with which it had longstanding connections. But reports said the family initially hoped to relocate there permanently and later concluded that such a move would be difficult because of the political implications of hosting Assad.The Damascus court's verdict is the first Syrian conviction against Assad himself. The court found him guilty of offences including premeditated and intentional murder, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity. His younger brother Maher was handed the same sentence in absentia.Maher commanded Syria's elite Fourth Armoured Division and was one of the most powerful military figures under Assad. The division was repeatedly accused by opposition activists and rights groups of involvement in crackdowns, killings and torture during the conflict.Assad's cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa province, was also sentenced to death. Unlike Assad and Maher, Najib was in Syrian custody and appeared in court wearing a prison uniform.Najib's role is particularly important because Deraa is widely regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 uprising against Assad. The unrest began after security forces detained and allegedly tortured teenagers who had written anti-government graffiti on a school wall.The crackdown that followed helped turn local protests into nationwide demonstrations. The government's violent response contributed to the escalation into an armed conflict that eventually drew in regional and global powers.The court also sentenced several other former military and security officials to death in absentia, including former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and former military intelligence chief in Deraa Louay al-Ali.The ruling was met with celebrations in parts of Syria, particularly in areas that suffered heavily under Assad's security forces.Crowds gathered outside the courthouse in Damascus, chanting and waving Syrian flags. In Deraa, families of people killed or detained during the early years of the uprising gathered with photographs of their relatives.For many victims, the verdict carried significance beyond the punishment itself. It was an official acknowledgement by Syria's new authorities of crimes committed during the Assad era.Noha al-Masri, a prosecutor involved in the case, lost her brother during the crackdown in Deraa in 2011."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."Reuters reported that the trial process lasted nearly four months and was presented by Syria's new authorities as part of a wider effort to pursue transitional justice after the fall of Assad.But the verdict has also drawn criticism from human rights groups over the fairness of the proceedings. The Associated Press reported that rights organisations raised concerns about whether the trials were rushed and whether defendants received adequate legal protections. Human Rights Watch also criticised the use of the death penalty, saying accountability requires a justice system capable of guaranteeing fair trials.For now, the answer appears to be no. The death sentence has no immediate practical effect on Assad because he is outside Syrian territory and under Russian protection. Syria would need Russia to surrender him or otherwise allow him to be transferred to Syrian custody.Anwar al-Bunni, head of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research, argued that the death sentence itself could make extradition harder."There is a huge problem, which is that no one will hand over a criminal to a country that issues a death sentence. This will cut off the road to Assad, and many other criminals, being handed over to Syria," Bunni told Reuters."This is performative justice, not transitional justice," he said.Syria's new authorities have previously sought accountability for Assad and senior figures from his government. The issue has also been part of the complicated relationship between Damascus and Moscow. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa travelled to Moscow in October 2025 for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Assad's extradition among the issues surrounding the relationship.Assad also faces legal action outside Syria. France has issued an arrest warrant against him over allegations connected to the bombing of a press centre in Homs in 2012, according to Reuters.Assad inherited the presidency in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had ruled Syria for nearly three decades. Bashar initially presented himself as a modernising leader, but his rule became increasingly associated with political repression and the security apparatus.The defining event of his presidency was the 2011 uprising. What began as protests demanding political change developed into a devastating civil war involving the Syrian government, opposition groups, extremist organisations and foreign powers. Russia intervened militarily in support of Assad in 2015, helping his forces regain territory and eventually reducing the opposition's hold over much of the country.For years, Assad appeared to have survived the war. Then, in late 2024, the balance changed with extraordinary speed.Forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa launched an offensive from northern Syria and advanced rapidly towards Damascus. On December 8, the capital fell and the Assad government collapsed.The man who had ruled Syria for more than two decades disappeared from the country and resurfaced in Moscow.Nearly two years later, a Syrian court has sentenced him to death. Yet the most important fact remains unchanged: Bashar al-Assad is not in a Syrian prison. He is in Russia, living under the protection of the country that stood by his regime during the civil war.His exact whereabouts in Moscow remain undisclosed. Reports have pointed to the elite Rublyovka district, while other details of his life suggest a tightly controlled existence away from politics and public view.The Damascus verdict therefore closes one chapter of Assad's rule, but not the question of whether the former Syrian president will ever return to the country he ruled for 24 years.For now, the death sentence exists on paper in Damascus while Assad remains thousands of kilometres away in Russia.
Article Summary: Bashar al-Assad was sentenced to death in absentia by a Syrian court. He was found guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity. Assad fled Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. He and his family were granted asylum in Russia, where they are believed to be living.

Article Title: Two American jets with same flight number avoid mid-air disaster
Article Text:
The two jets were kept at different altitudes and remained safely separated as they passed through the same area.

How the disaster was averted

Why were both planes using the same flight number

A potential aviation disaster was narrowly avoided near Phoenix after an air traffic controller noticed that two American Airlines jets were operating under the same flight number while approaching and departing the airport at almost the same time.The incident happened shortly after midnight on Friday, when an American Airlines flight arriving from Chicago was approaching Phoenix as another aircraft assigned the same flight number was preparing to depart. Both aircraft were identified as American 2482, creating the risk of confusion as their flight paths converged.Audio of the incident, posted by ATC.com, captures the controller repeatedly referring to the aircraft as “American 2482 on the arrival” and “American 2482 on the departure”. This allowed the pilots to distinguish between the two aircraft as the controller issued instructions.The arriving aircraft was kept above the departing jet as their flight paths crossed. The controller also instructed the departing aircraft not to climb too high, preserving a safe vertical gap between the two planes. Both pilots were able to see the other aircraft while they were still several miles apart.After the aircraft had safely passed each other, the arriving pilot praised the controller, telling him it was “nice work”.“It could have been disastrous, but I’m glad it worked out,” the controller replied.The controller later said he had worked in air traffic control for 25 years and had never seen two aircraft “pretty much merge with the same call sign”.Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the incident likely resulted from an overlap that was not detected by the airline’s dispatch operation. Both the dispatcher and pilots would normally review and approve the flight plans, making it unusual for two aircraft with the same flight number to be scheduled to occupy the same airspace at the same time.“You can drop the ball and that shouldn’t happen, but it’s nice to see that the system is resilient and we have all the safeguards,” Arroyo said. He added that he had encountered a similar problem only a few times during his four decades with United Airlines.Flight 2482 regularly operates between Chicago and Phoenix. The Chicago-bound aircraft had been delayed by bad weather, while American Airlines had arranged for another aircraft in Phoenix to operate the scheduled departure on time. This resulted in both aircraft briefly sharing the same airspace.
Article Summary: Two American Airlines jets were operating under the same flight number while approaching and departing the airport at almost the same time. Both aircraft were identified as American 2482, creating the risk of confusion as their flight paths converged. Both pilots were able to see the other aircraft while they were still several miles apart. The arriving pilot praised the controller, telling him it was “nice work”

Article Title: ‘Pretty soon’: Trump vows to claim Hormuz as US territory; Iran hits back
Article Text:
Trump’s remarks came days after he claimed that the US had “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz and described the American naval blockade as a “WALL OF STEEL”.

US President Donald Trump Friday said the United States will soon declare the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz a territory of the US, escalating his rhetoric over the waterway at the centre of the ongoing conflict with Iran.“After we finish defeating Iran… I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said at a rally in New York on Friday. He did not explain how such a declaration would be implemented or what legal implications it would have.Trump’s remarks came days after he claimed that the US had “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz and described the American naval blockade as a “WALL OF STEEL”. The waterway is a critical route for global oil and gas shipments, and disruptions to shipping through it have already pushed up concerns over energy supplies and prices.Iran rejected Trump’s threat with deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi saying the strategic waterway will remain under Tehran’s control.Gharibabadi said Iran would decide when the strait is opened or closed and would maintain what it described as a blockade until Washington accepts its “strategic defeat”.“Once and for all, accept the reality: up to this point, you have suffered strategic and heavy defeats; the Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian; this strait will only be closed and opened under Iran's command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and cease your fanciful delusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” he posted on X.The comments also came as tensions remained high between Washington and Tehran, with the US continuing its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Trump said the blockade meant that “No ships get through unless we want them to”.Trump has repeatedly claimed that Iran has been severely weakened by the conflict, while acknowledging that it retains some missile and drone capabilities. “They still have missiles, but not a lot. They still have drones, but just a fraction of what they had,” he said.He added that Iran’s “manufacturing of missiles is 82 percent” and that its manufacturing capacity was “largely gone.” Trump also claimed that “159 ships are right now at the bottom of the sea” and said Iran had 212 aircraft, adding that “every one of their airplanes is shot down.”Trump again defended the US military campaign, saying the United States was “winning big with the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He also reiterated his opposition to Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon, saying: “If we didn’t hit them, you would have had a nuclear weapon,” and adding: “They’re never going to have a nuclear weapon.”The situation in the Strait has meanwhile become more volatile. Two tankers operated by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil company ADNOC were attacked by drones while transiting the waterway on Thursday. No casualties were reported, but the attacks caused minor damage and prompted the UAE to accuse Iran of piracy and a violation of freedom of navigation.The attacks have further reduced commercial traffic through the strait, through which a significant share of the world's oil supply normally passes. Iran has continued to restrict shipping, while the US has maintained its blockade and warned of further economic pressure on Tehran.
Article Summary: “After we finish defeating Iran… I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said at a rally in New York on Friday. He did not explain how such a declaration would be implemented or what legal implications it would have.

Article Title: Frederick clears way for Sanjay Govil’s Washington Freedom cricket stadium
Article Text:
Washington Freedom in action during a Major League Cricket match in Morrisville, N.C., in July 2024. The franchise went on to win its maiden MLC title that season and is now poised to get its own stadium in Frederick, Md. (Photo: The American Bazaar)

Major League Cricket (MLC) powerhouse Washington Freedom is poised to get a permanent home in suburban Washington after the Frederick City Council approved the rezoning of roughly 24 acres for a 10,000-seat cricket stadium, a milestone that could significantly boost the sport’s growth in the nation’s capital region.The City Council voted 5-1 last week, with one member absent, to rezone the Gateway Property on Frederick’s eastern edge between Route 144 and Interstate 70. The site, currently a golf driving range, is expected to become the home of the Washington Freedom, the MLC franchise owned by Indian American entrepreneur Sanjay Govil.Frederick, located about 30 miles northwest of Washington, D.C., is Maryland’s second-largest city after Baltimore. Home to about 80,000 residents, it is part of the Washington metropolitan area.For Govil, the council’s decision marks a pivotal step toward giving both the franchise and the region’s growing cricket community a stadium they can finally call their own.“I think it’s huge because it’s a lot easier and faster to build the support of the local community if you have a stadium, which is local, and we have people who actually come and watch the Freedom team,” Govil told The American Bazaar.“They didn’t have that luxury in the past because we were playing in other locations. So getting this approval from the council is a very big step toward building a stadium.”Govil, founder of the Maryland-headquartered technology company Infinite Computer Solutions, said the franchise hopes construction can move quickly, although several regulatory steps remain before work can begin.“Obviously, we would love to play in 2027 and be part of the Olympics in 2028 in some capacity,” he said. “But we still have a few steps to go through. We’ll work closely with the city, the county, the state, and all the relevant authorities to move as fast as possible.”For the first time since 1900, cricket is set to return to the Olympic Games at Los Angeles in 2028.For Govil and the Washington Freedom, the rezoning represents more than a real estate milestone. It is the beginning of what they hope will become a long-term home for both professional and grassroots cricket in the nation’s capital region.A dedicated stadium would provide young cricketers in Maryland with a place to train, give local clubs access to world-class infrastructure, and allow fans to experience elite cricket close to home. It could also help establish the Washington region as one of cricket’s leading centers in the United States.The proposed facility is designed as more than a venue for professional cricket. Plans call for a cricket park and multi-use community space, with year-round public access and opportunities for youth sports, recreation, community events, and other activities. Project supporters have emphasized preserving green space while creating a destination where local residents can engage with cricket beyond the Major League Cricket season.If completed as planned, it would likely become only the second purpose-built full-fledged cricket stadium on the East Coast after Broward County Stadium in Fort Lauderdale. Govil said the project also stands apart because it is being built on privately owned land.“If you talk about a full-fledged stadium, probably the second on the East Coast,” said Govil, who also co-owns Welsh Fire, which competes in the English cricket league Hundred. “The big distinguishing factor we have is that we’re building a stadium on private land. I think that’s probably the first in the country.”The stadium is expected to host cricket from April through October while also accommodating youth sports, festivals, concerts, artisan markets, graduation ceremonies, and other community events during the rest of the year. City officials estimate the facility could attract about 100,000 visitors annually and generate nearly $2 million in tax revenue each year.For the growing cricket community in Maryland and the wider Washington metropolitan area, the stadium could provide something the region has long lacked: a dedicated, professional-grade cricket venue close to its large South Asian and Caribbean communities.The Washington metropolitan area is home to one of the largest and most active amateur cricket communities in the United States, with dozens of leagues, hundreds of teams, and thousands of players. Yet despite the sport’s popularity, the region has never had a permanent professional cricket stadium.“Cricket has always been a big part of my life, so it’s really exciting to see the sport continue to grow in this area,” said Shravan Sudhir, who plays for Fairfax Cricket Club in the Washington Cricket League Premier Division.“Having a dedicated stadium in Frederick is important because it gives the sport a real home and creates a place where players, families, and fans can come together. Its approval is a great step forward and will hopefully create even more opportunities for players and the wider cricket community.”For Falgun Patel, a board member of the Maryland Youth Cricket Association, coach of Maryland’s first state cricket team, and president of the Howard County Cricket League, the approval represents the culmination of years of grassroots work.“It is the realization of a dream that so many volunteers, players, families, and cricket lovers have worked and hoped for over the years,” Patel said.“Having been involved in growing youth and adult cricket for many years, it makes me incredibly proud and emotional to see our community finally take this step and create a place where future generations can play, grow, and call home.”The move is particularly significant for Washington Freedom, which has emerged as one of Major League Cricket’s premier franchises.The Freedom won its maiden MLC championship in 2024, defeating the San Francisco Unicorns by 96 runs in the final. The team returned to the championship match in 2025 but lost to MI New York by five runs. In 2026, the Freedom again reached the final before falling to the Los Angeles Knight Riders by a single run at the Oakland Coliseum.Three consecutive championship appearances—including the 2024 title—have established Washington Freedom as one of Major League Cricket’s hottest franchises.Govil credited the team’s sustained success to its culture, coaching, and fan support.“I think it’s the culture, the team performance, the coaching we have, and the strong support from the fans,” he said. “We have created a culture where people play in a fearless fashion.”He also acknowledged that success in a league where talent is evenly distributed often comes down to the smallest of margins.“All teams are very good, and there’s always an element of luck,” Govil said. “A couple of injuries here, one play there, and you can be on either side.”The Frederick project also marks another step in Major League Cricket’s broader transition toward dedicated home venues. During its early seasons, the league relied largely on shared or temporary facilities.The Texas Super Kings play at Grand Prairie Stadium in Texas, a city-owned facility operated by American Cricket Enterprises. The Los Angeles Knight Riders opened the purpose-built Knight Riders Cricket Ground at Fairplex in Pomona in 2026, while the San Francisco Unicorns have used the Oakland Coliseum as their home venue, which has also hosted MLC playoff and championship matches.The Washington Freedom stadium would add another dedicated cricket destination to the league’s growing infrastructure while giving the franchise a permanent identity in the Washington market.(By arrangement with The American Bazaar
Article Summary: Frederick City Council approved rezoning of roughly 24 acres for a 10,000-seat cricket stadium. Site, currently a golf driving range, is expected to become the home of the Washington Freedom, the MLC franchise owned by Indian American entrepreneur Sanjay Govil. City officials estimate the facility could attract about 100,000 visitors annually.

Article Title: An unthinkable crime shatters an Indian family in US— and raises questions about AI
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

TOI Corrrespondent from Washington:

Before police found his mother and younger brother dead inside their quiet suburban home in Acton, outside Boston, 17-year-old Arjun Aravind had allegedly been exploring a dark world online - using the internet and ChatGPT to search for ideas and create fictional scenarios about killing his own family.That revelation, disclosed by local District Attorney Marian Ryan, has transformed an already horrific double homicide into a case with an unsettling 21st-century dimension: the intersection of troubled youth and digital conversations on tap in the age of artificial intelligence.Aravind is accused of killing his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, at their home on Tuesday. He faces two counts of murder, along with assault and battery and motor-vehicle charges. A not-guilty plea was entered on his behalf on Thursday, and he was ordered held without bail while undergoing a mental-health evaluation after he was brought to the court in handcuffs and leg shackles.Ryan said Aravind had recently displayed “concerning behavior,” including using the internet and ChatGPT to develop “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family.”She disclosed he had created what appeared to be Gothic-novel-style stories, asking questions and creating characters whose circumstances seemed connected to threats against his family.Police were summoned after Aravind's father Sukumaran could not reach his family and a tutor arriving for a scheduled appointment could not get into the house. Officers found Siddharth on the first floor and his mother in the basement, both dead with trauma injuries after signs of struggle. Aravind allegedly fled in his mother's Honda Accord and was found inside the car in neighboring Wayland early Wednesday when he was arrested without incident.The case is particularly jarring for Indian-American families because such killings remain rare, although there is a haunting precedent in the Washington area. In March 2005, Jayant Kadian, then a 20-year-old college student, killed his mother, Kiran Kadian - whose husband Rajesh Kadian, a strategic affairs commentator, was a familiar figure in think-tank circles in the Capital - at the family's Virginia home. Kiran was stabbed repeatedly while preparing food. Jayant later pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and received a 20-year prison sentence.There is no credible national database showing how frequently matricide or patricide occurs specifically among Indian-Americans. National research shows that parricide - a child killing a parent - itself is relatively rare; a major study found matricide constitutes less than 2 percent of US homicides in which the victim-offender relationship is known.But what makes the Acton case especially alarming is that investigators have encountered something previous generations of cops and prosecutors could scarcely have imagined: an alleged killer leaving behind conversations with a machine about violent fantasies. That matters because young people are increasingly turning to AI for advice and emotional support.A recent study found that one in eight adolescents and young adults reported using generative AI for mental-health advice. Researchers have warned that current AI safety evaluations may miss dangers arising in real-world interactions with vulnerable youth. At the same time, social-media companies face scores of lawsuits alleging that their platforms can contribute to harmful effects on young people, allegations the companies dispute.In the Acton killings, however, the technological debate is secondary for now to a family and community tragedy. As Ryan put it, the community and the school system were entering “a very dark and long process.”
Article Summary: 17-year-old Arjun Aravind is accused of killing his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth, 14, at their home on Tuesday. He faces two counts of murder, along with assault and battery and motor-vehicle charges. A not-guilty plea was entered on his behalf on Thursday.

Article Title: An entrepreneur spent $1.4 million buying a 300-acre California ghost town, then moved in and began rebuilding it as a business
Article Text:
Representative Image of a restored historic mining town with 19th-century buildings and mountain scenery (AI-generated image)

How a $1.4 million bid won the race for California's ghost town

What Underwood found on 300 acres of remote, largely untouched 19th-century mining infrastructure

Why a fire in June 2020 destroyed the town's centrepiece hotel less than two years after Underwood bought the property

Why turning a ghost town into a working business has taken years of rebuilding, and counting

In July 2018, entrepreneur Brent Underwood, along with business partner Jon Bier, purchased the abandoned mining town of Cerro Gordo in California's Inyo Mountains for $1.4 million. The deal, which closed on Friday the 13th, included more than 300 acres of land and 22 surviving structures, among them a 19th-century hotel, a bunkhouse and a former superintendent's house. Cerro Gordo had first grown into a boomtown after silver was discovered there in 1865, at one point becoming one of California's largest producers of silver and lead, before falling prices and a fire pushed the town toward abandonment by the late 1870s. Underwood, who had previously run a hostel in Austin, Texas, saw an opportunity to turn the deserted property into a hospitality destination while preserving its history, a project that would go on to consume his life savings and, eventually, his full-time residence. Underwood's journey stands as a striking example of how ambitious historical restoration rarely unfolds according to plan, requiring years of unexpected setbacks, financial strain and stubborn persistence before a long-abandoned town can genuinely come back to life.Underwood and Bier were not the only ones interested in Cerro Gordo when it went up for sale. According to real estate agent Jake Rasmuson, who handled the listing, the property drew about a dozen offers after going on the market at an asking price of $ 925,000, with some competing bids reportedly higher than the $1.4 million Underwood and Bier ultimately paid. The sellers, a trust made up of brothers who had inherited the property after it stayed in family hands for decades, chose the pair's offer specifically because their plan prioritised preserving the town's history and keeping it accessible to the public, rather than simply developing the land for private use. Underwood has said the purchase used every penny of his personal savings, supplemented by a loan and a handful of small contributions from friends who wanted to be part of the project.Cerro Gordo sits in a remote stretch of the Inyo Mountains, reachable only by a mix of paved and dirt roads roughly 25 miles from Lone Pine, the nearest town with a grocery store. At its peak in the 1870s, the town supported a population of around 4,000 residents drawn by its silver and lead mining operations, but by the time Underwood took ownership, only a single caretaker remained on site. The 22 surviving structures had been protected from looting and the elements for decades under the previous family's stewardship, leaving Underwood with a largely intact, if deteriorating, collection of 19th-century buildings to work with, including mine shafts extending hundreds of feet underground that once anchored the town's entire economy.Underwood's restoration plans suffered a severe setback less than two years into the project. In the early hours of June 15, 2020, a fire broke out at the American Hotel, a building that had first opened its doors on that same date back in 1871. The blaze destroyed the hotel completely, along with an adjoining icehouse and a nearby residence once known as the home of a notorious 19th-century killer. No injuries were reported, and investigators later pointed to the building's old electrical wiring, combined with decades-old newspapers stuffed into the walls as insulation, as the likely cause. Underwood has described the fire as one of the most devastating moments of his life, since the hotel had stood as both the literal and symbolic centre of his plans to revive the town.Rather than a quick renovation, Underwood's plan to convert Cerro Gordo into a hospitality and tourism destination has stretched across years, complicated significantly by the loss of the American Hotel. In the years following the fire, work shifted toward reconstructing the hotel essentially from the ground up rather than simply restoring an existing structure, a rebuild that was reportedly completed by 2025. Progress across the wider property has also been slowed by the site's remoteness, particularly the lack of a reliable water source, a challenge Underwood has addressed through temporary measures like trucked-in water and pumping operations drawing from deep within the old mine shafts. Since March 2020, Underwood has lived at Cerro Gordo full time, documenting the town's slow transformation, including the fire and its aftermath, for a large online audience, turning what began as a real estate purchase into an ongoing, very public restoration project still working toward its original goal of welcoming paying visitors to stay.
Article Summary: Brent Underwood and business partner Jon Bier bought Cerro Gordo in July 2018 for $1.4 million. The property includes more than 300 acres of land and 22 surviving structures, among them a 19th-century hotel, a bunkhouse and a former superintendent's house. In June 2020, a fire broke out at the American Hotel, which had first opened its doors in 1871. Underwood has described the fire as one of the most devastating moments of his life, since the hotel had stood as both the literal and symbolic centre of his plans to revive the town.

Article Title: In 1974, Vietnam veteran Kenneth Deardorff moved to Alaska looking for work; 14 years later, he became the last person in US history to receive a homestead title
Article Text:
Kenneth Deardorff's journey from Vietnam veteran to Alaska homesteader

Life on a remote homestead along the Stony River

From clearing the land to completing the homestead requirements

Why Deardorff had to wait until 1988 for his title

The last person to receive a Homestead Act title

Vietnam veteran Kenneth Deardorff arrived in Alaska in 1974 with a geography degree and plans to find work with the US Geological Survey or another employer. Instead, the California native became fascinated by the idea of building a life in the state's remote wilderness. He travelled to the Bureau of Land Management office in Anchorage, learned about homesteading and eventually claimed land along the Stony River in southwestern Alaska. The decision changed the course of his life. Deardorff settled in an isolated area with no nearby roads, hunted and trapped for income and operated a small general store while developing his property. He completed the requirements for his homestead in 1979, but his government patent did not arrive until May 5, 1988. By then, the Homestead Act had ended for new claims in Alaska. The document made Deardorff the last person in US history to receive a homestead title under the law.Born near Los Angeles, Deardorff joined the US Army after high school and served in Vietnam, where he was wounded in action. After leaving the military, he returned to California and earned a college degree in geography. In 1974, he travelled to Alaska, initially looking for employment and hoping his education could lead to work with the US Geological Survey or another organisation.His plans changed after he became interested in the federal homesteading programme. Deardorff visited the Bureau of Land Management office in Anchorage to learn about available land and eventually established a homestead claim along the Stony River in southwestern Alaska. Rather than pursuing the conventional career he had originally imagined, he chose to build a new life in one of the country's most remote regions.Deardorff's new home was far removed from the towns and roads of California. His homestead along the Stony River had no nearby road connecting it to the outside world, making even routine travel a difficult undertaking. He relied on boats, aircraft and long journeys on foot to reach other communities. Mail could arrive only about once a month, and collecting it required travelling to another village. Despite these challenges, Deardorff worked to make the property sustainable and developed several ways to support himself. He hunted and trapped furs and established a small general store on his property for people travelling along the Stony River. These activities helped him earn an income while he continued improving the land and building his isolated homestead.Building a successful homestead required much more than simply occupying the property. Deardorff had to improve and develop the land while meeting the legal requirements of the Homestead Act. He completed those requirements in 1979, after years of work in the remote Alaskan wilderness. One of the most unusual parts of that effort involved a 1945 Allis-Chalmers Model C tractor that he acquired in 1976. Because there were no roads to his property, the tractor was dismantled and transported by aircraft in three separate loads before being hauled the remaining distance by dog sled. Once reassembled, Deardorff used it to help clear the land, including pulling tree stumps. His work eventually allowed him to fulfil the requirements for his homestead.Although Deardorff completed the requirements for his homestead in 1979, the government did not issue his final patent for another nine years. The delay was particularly remarkable because the Homestead Act was already nearing the end of its long history. The Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 ended homesteading in the lower 48 states but gave Alaska a special 10-year extension. New homestead claims in Alaska could therefore continue until 1986. Deardorff's claim had been filed in 1974, allowing his case to continue through the government process after the programme ended for new claims. On May 5, 1988, he finally received his federal homestead patent, completing a process that had begun 14 years earlier when he first arrived in Alaska.Deardorff's 1988 patent eventually became more than a document proving ownership of his remote Alaskan property. Historical research completed in 2001 established that he was the final person to obtain title to a homesteaded property under the Homestead Act. The National Archives also identifies his May 5, 1988 patent as the final homestead awarded under the legislation. His story therefore became the closing chapter of a programme that had begun with the Homestead Act of 1862 and helped encourage settlement across large parts of the American West. Deardorff later donated objects connected to his life as a homesteader, including his original patent and other belongings, to Homestead National Historical Park. His tractor was recovered from Alaska in 2017 and preserved, leaving behind physical reminders of America's final homesteading story.
Article Summary: Kenneth Deardorff arrived in Alaska in 1974 with plans to work with the US Geological Survey. Instead, he became fascinated by the idea of building a life in the state's remote wilderness. He settled in an isolated area with no nearby roads, hunted and trapped for income and operated a small general store. He completed the requirements for his homestead in 1979, but his government patent did not arrive until May 5, 1988. By then, the Homestead Act had ended for new claims in Alaska.

Article Title: In 1870, a former slave and Union soldier staked a homestead in Nebraska; drought and grasshoppers cost him the claim, but he eventually owned more than 2,000 acres
Article Text:
Homestead soddy in Box Butte County. Source: History Nebraska - Nebraska.gov

Escape from slavery and Civil War service

From Slavery to Affluence: Memoirs of Robert Anderson, Ex-Slave

Early farming failure in Nebraska

African American Homesteaders in the Great Plains

Building capital and acquiring western land

Legacy and historical record

In 1870, Robert Ball Anderson, a former slave and Union Army veteran, filed a claim for a 160-acre homestead in Butler County, Nebraska. Severe drought and grasshopper swarms destroyed his crops, forcing him to give up the property.Instead of abandoning his goals, Anderson spent years working as a railroad cook and farmhand to rebuild his savings. He later moved to Box Butte County in the Nebraska Panhandle, where he built a farm of more than 2,000 acres.According to historical records from History Nebraska and the National Park Service about African American homesteaders on the Great Plains, Anderson became one of the largest landowners in western Nebraska. He overcame natural disasters, financial losses, and racial discrimination to build his agricultural estate.Anderson was born into slavery on 1 March 1843 on the Ball plantation in Green County, Kentucky. In his autobiography,, he described his childhood in small log cabins where enslaved families lived "pretty much as pigs in a pen."When Anderson was six, his mother was sold to a slave trader.He never saw her again. After years of physical abuse that left deep scars on his back, Anderson decided to escape.In the autumn of 1864, during the American Civil War, Anderson told his owner that he planned to join the Union Army. He walked 20 miles to enlist and became a soldier in the 125th United States Colored Infantry.After the war ended, Anderson completed his military service at several posts across the American frontier. His assignments included Fort Leavenworth in Kansas and military posts in New Mexico, Texas, and Colorado.After receiving an honourable discharge from the army, Anderson moved to Iowa. He worked in a local brickyard and as a hired farmhand.The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to citizens or people intending to become citizens who agreed to live on and improve the land for five years. Seeking financial independence, Anderson moved to Butler County, Nebraska, in 1870 and filed his first homestead claim.His first attempt at farming failed because of severe natural conditions. Years of drought and large grasshopper infestations during the 1870s destroyed crops across the Great Plains. Anderson eventually had to give up his claim.The National Park Service's articlenotes that many Black and white homesteaders abandoned their claims during this difficult period. Anderson, however, chose to stay in the region and rebuild his finances.To earn money again, Anderson spent three years working as a farmhand in Kansas. He later returned to Nebraska and worked as a cook for railroad construction crews.By 1884, he had saved $1,600. He then moved to the sparsely settled Box Butte County in the Nebraska Panhandle. There, he filed another homestead claim, built a sod house, and later added a log cabin.Anderson soon faced another serious setback. A man who had borrowed his $1,600 savings left the state without repaying him. Anderson was once again left without money.He took out personal loans to keep his farm operating and spent the next decade paying off his debts through hard manual work.Records in the History Nebraska collection (RG2973.AM) show that Anderson continued acquiring land through homestead and timber culture claims as well as direct purchases. Over the years, these efforts steadily increased his property holdings.By the early twentieth century, Anderson owned more than 2,000 acres of valuable farmland in Box Butte County. His farm was fully equipped and included horses, cattle, and modern machinery.Looking back on his life in his memoir, Anderson wrote: "A slave at the age of twenty, penniless at the age of forty-five, I am a rich man today."On 19 March 1922, when he was 79, Anderson married 21-year-old schoolteacher Daisy Graham. She helped him dictate and prepare his life story for publication.Anderson died on 30 November 1930 at the age of 87 after a motor vehicle accident near Union, Nebraska. He was buried in Hemingford Cemetery in Box Butte County.His life remains an important example of African American landownership on the Great Plains. His records show how, despite slavery, poverty, natural disasters, financial setbacks, and racial prejudice, Anderson built one of the largest African American-owned farms in western Nebraska.
Article Summary: Robert Ball Anderson was born into slavery in Green County, Kentucky. He served in the Union Army during the American Civil War. In 1870, Anderson filed a claim for a 160-acre homestead in Butler County, Nebraska. Severe drought and grasshopper swarms destroyed his crops, forcing him to give up the property. He spent years working as a railroad cook and farmhand to rebuild his savings. He later moved to Box Butte County in the Nebraska Panhandle, and built a farm of more than 2,000 acres.

Article Title: California has added more than 50,000 tons of gravel to a river below Keswick Dam since 2022 to help endangered salmon lay eggs
Article Text:
Representative Image of a narrow stretch of river flowing below Keswick Dam (AI-generated image)

Why Shasta and Keswick Dams cut off winter run Chinook salmon from their historic Sacramento River spawning grounds entirely

How gravel injection projects have worked to rebuild spawning habitat lost to decades of dam operation

Why this restoration work remains a permanent, recurring commitment rather than a one-time fix

Below Keswick Dam on California's Sacramento River, salmon face a problem the dam itself created. Winter run Chinook salmon, now listed as endangered, once spawned across hundreds of miles of cold mountain streams before Shasta and Keswick Dams cut off access to that historic habitat entirely. Confined now to a much shorter stretch of river just below the dams, the fish depend on gravel beds to lay their eggs, yet the dam also blocks the natural flow of gravel that would normally replenish those beds over time. Since 2022 alone, state and federal agencies have responded by trucking in and placing more than 50,000 tons of gravel into the river near Keswick Dam, an ongoing effort aimed at rebuilding the spawning habitat the dam had quietly stripped away. This effort illustrates a broader reality of managing rivers reshaped by dams, that undoing decades of blocked natural processes often requires sustained, ongoing human intervention rather than a single restorative fix, especially for species with nowhere else left to spawn.Winter run Chinook salmon are unusual among Pacific salmon species because they spawn during the summer months, which means their eggs need consistently cold water to survive California's hot Central Valley heat.According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's account of the species, Shasta and Keswick Dams block winter run Chinook salmon from their historical habitat entirely, confining the population to the lower reaches of the Sacramento River below the dams, where summer air temperatures can average nearly 100 degrees Fahrenheit. That confinement leaves the fish reliant on cold water releases managed from Shasta Lake and on a much narrower stretch of river for spawning than the species evolved to use, making the quality of that remaining habitat especially critical to the population's survival.Because dams trap the natural sediment that would otherwise replenish riverbed gravel downstream, agencies have turned to physically trucking gravel to the site and placing it directly into the river, a process known as gravel augmentation. According to a project update from Reclamation District 108, issued jointly with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the United States Bureau of Reclamation, this work has continued steadily in recent years, with gravel augmentation projects near Keswick Dam adding more than 50,000 tons of rock to the upper Sacramento River since 2022 alone. The United States Bureau of Reclamation has also directed multimillion-dollar funding awards toward similar gravel and side channel restoration work stretching from Keswick Dam down to the Feather River confluence, reflecting how central this single stretch of river has become to the species' broader recovery strategy. Individual placements have ranged from around 20,000 tons added below Keswick Dam in a single project to smaller top-up placements of 5,000 tons in subsequent years, with agencies returning to the same general site repeatedly rather than treating any one delivery as a final fix.Unlike a natural river system, where gravel constantly cycles downstream and gets replenished by erosion further upstream, the stretch below Keswick Dam has no such supply once the dam blocks that process, meaning any gravel placed into the river will eventually wash downstream and need to be replaced again. California Department of Fish and Wildlife environmental scientist Matt Johnson has said this dynamic is well understood by the agencies involved, noting that river flows will continue to push newly placed gravel downstream over time, which is precisely why the work must continue periodically rather than functioning as a single completed project. With winter run Chinook salmon now dependent almost entirely on this kind of artificially maintained spawning habitat, California's gravel injection program has effectively become a permanent piece of infrastructure, one that officials say offers the endangered species its best remaining chance to reproduce successfully within the small stretch of river still available to it below the dam.
Article Summary: Winter run Chinook salmon, now listed as endangered, once spawned across hundreds of miles of cold mountain streams. Shasta and Keswick Dams cut off access to that historic habitat entirely. Confined now to a much shorter stretch of river just below the dams, the fish depend on gravel beds to lay their eggs. Dam also blocks the natural flow of gravel that would normally replenish those beds over time.

Article Title: In 1968, a California landowner demanded $100 an acre for land inside Pinnacles that officials valued at $17; a year later the Park Service paid more than $46 an acre and bought the parcel for $7,400
Article Text:
In 1968, a California landowner demanded $100 an acre for land inside Pinnacles that officials valued at $17;

Commercial enterprise caused federal conflict

The Heart of the Gabilans: An Administrative History of Pinnacles National Monument

Years of talks led to a buyout

Pioneer settlement shaped property rights

Article Title: Home Depot billionaire Bernie Marcus' foundation donates $28.7 million to stem cell research that could repair hearts damaged by heart attacks
Article Text:
Home Depot founder donates $28.7 million to advance stem cell research

How stem cells could repair heart damage

Gene editing could help make the treatment safer

Bernie Marcus' lifelong connection to medicine

The Marcus Foundation's long history of medical giving

The foundation of late Home Depot cofounder Bernie Marcus has committed $28.7 million to stem cell research at the University of Southern California. The research aims to develop treatments for heart damage caused by heart attacks. The funding will support physician-scientist Charles “Chuck” Murry, director of USC’s Stem Cell Center. His team is studying how stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells could help regenerate damaged cardiac tissue. The work is still experimental and is being developed towards clinical trials. It is not yet an established treatment for heart attack patients. The donation also continues Marcus’ long history of supporting medical research, a cause that had a personal connection to him because he had once dreamed of becoming a doctor.The Marcus Foundation has committed $28.7 million to support Murry’s research into regenerative treatments for damaged hearts. USC says his work focuses on using stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells to repair tissue damaged by heart attacks, while the foundation said the funding will help advance gene-edited cellular therapy towards clinical trials. The gift is the largest the Marcus Foundation has given to USC and one of its largest contributions to academic medicine.A heart attack can destroy part of the heart muscle when blood flow is blocked, leaving behind scar tissue that can weaken the organ and reduce its pumping ability. Researchers are studying whether new heart muscle cells created from stem cells could replace some of the lost tissue and help restore cardiac function.The human heart has a limited ability to replace muscle cells after major injury, which is why researchers have been exploring regenerative medicine as a possible treatment for heart disease. Murry’s work focuses on cardiomyocytes, the specialised muscle cells responsible for the heart’s contractions. Scientists can produce these cells from stem cells in the laboratory and study whether they can survive after being transplanted into damaged heart tissue, integrate with existing cells and contribute to the heart’s function. However, the treatment remains experimental and faces several challenges. Researchers must determine how effectively the new cells work in humans and whether they can be safely introduced without causing complications.A major challenge with transplanting new heart muscle cells is the risk of abnormal heart rhythms if the cells do not beat in sync with the patient's existing heart tissue. Murry’s team has explored gene-editing techniques designed to address this problem before the cells are transplanted. USC has reported promising preclinical findings from animal studies in which gene-edited cells reduced the risk of dangerous arrhythmias and helped restore damaged heart tissue. However, these findings do not prove that the treatment is safe or effective in humans. Clinical trials will be required to determine whether the approach can eventually be used as a treatment for people who have suffered heart attacks, and the Marcus Foundation's funding is intended to help move the research closer to that stage.Marcus had dreamed of becoming a doctor before he became a billionaire businessman. His family could not afford medical school, so he instead studied pharmacy at Rutgers University and graduated in 1954. According to Home Depot, Marcus sometimes skipped classes to sell Amana freezers door-to-door while studying. He later moved into business and held senior positions at several companies before being fired from Handy Dan, a home improvement retailer, in 1978. The setback led Marcus and Arthur Blank to establish Home Depot with other partners, opening the first stores in Atlanta in 1979. The company eventually grew into one of the largest home improvement retailers in the US. Marcus died on November 4, 2024, at the age of 95, with Forbes estimating his fortune at about $11 billion.Marcus and his wife, Billi, established The Marcus Foundation in 1989, and the foundation says it has since awarded more than $2.7 billion through more than 3,500 grants. Medical research is one of its main areas of focus, with priorities including stem cell research and regenerative medicine, cancer detection and treatment, autism, integrative medicine and cardiovascular disease, including stroke. Its past medical initiatives include the Marcus Stroke and Neuroscience Center at Grady, the Marcus Autism Center and the Marcus Institute for Brain Health at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. The latest USC donation continues that decades-long focus on medicine. While stem-cell-based heart regeneration is still experimental, the $28.7 million commitment could help researchers determine whether the technology can eventually become a safe treatment for heart tissue damaged by heart attacks.
Article Summary: The Marcus Foundation has committed $28.7 million to support research into regenerative treatments for damaged hearts. Researchers are studying whether new heart muscle cells created from stem cells could replace some of the lost tissue and help restore cardiac function. The work is still experimental and is being developed towards clinical trials. It is not yet an established treatment for heart attack patients.

Article Title: 'Water is our red line': Shehbaz Sharif threatens India with 'direct response' over Indus Treaty

Shehbaz Sharif speaking on eve of Pakistan's Independence Day

Pakistan has yet again raked up India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), with its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatening a “direct response” to New Delhi’s move, which came days after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year."The Prime Minister said that India has proven itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. He announced that every drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. There will be no compromise on the water issue. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly," the Pakistani premier added.The military hostilities ended on May 10 after Islamabad sought a ceasefire following India’s air strikes on multiple Pakistani air bases.The conflict erupted after India's Operation Sindoor in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack.New Delhi kept the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance after a Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) meeting on April 23, 2025, and asserted that the conditions under which the treaty was negotiated have "fundamentally changed."India has asserted the treaty can no longer function in its present form and will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ends its support for cross-border terrorism.The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in September 1960.
