Article Title: Why US is questioning Pakistan's Rs 3 trillion defence spending
Article Text:
The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period (representative image)

US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency

Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion

Defence spending remains a key transparency concern

The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also raising concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing the executive budget proposal.The concerns were highlighted in the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, which assessed Pakistan's public financial transparency and identified gaps in the country's budgetary and fiscal disclosure practices.The report noted that Pakistan made its enacted budget and end-of-year financial statements widely available online. However, it said military and intelligence budgets remained outside adequate parliamentary or civilian public scrutiny.“The military and intelligence budgets were not subject to adequate parliamentary or civilian public oversight,” the report said.The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period.According to the assessment, this limits the time available for lawmakers and civil society to examine government spending before the budget is adopted.The state department called for three key changes to Pakistan's fiscal transparency framework.It urged Islamabad to make its executive budget proposal publicly available within a reasonable period, disclose detailed information about government debt obligations, including liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises, and bring military and intelligence agency budgets under parliamentary or civilian public oversight.The report also raised concerns about Pakistan's disclosure of public debt, saying only limited information was available on debt obligations, including those of major state-owned enterprises.At the same time, the US assessment acknowledged some positive aspects of Pakistan's public financial system.It said the country's supreme audit institution met international standards of independence and noted that its audit reports were published in a timely manner and contained substantive findings.The US assessment comes against the backdrop of a substantial increase in Pakistan's defence allocation for the 2026-27 financial year.In June, Pakistan's federal government proposed allocating Rs 3 trillion for defence services, up 17.65 per cent from the previous year's initial allocation of Rs 2.55 trillion, according to Dawn.The proposed defence services allocation amounts to about 2.08 per cent of Pakistan's projected GDP of Rs 143.6 trillion and nearly 16 per cent of the federal government's total outlay of Rs 18.77 trillion.Spending on civil works related to military infrastructure was projected to rise 7.92 per cent to Rs 363.16 billion, from Rs 336.49 billion previously.Military pensions are accounted for separately from the main defence services budget. The government has allocated Rs 822 billion for retired military personnel under the federal pension outlay, according to Dawn.The allocation for defence administration was set at Rs 10.9 billion, compared with Rs 7.9 billion in the outgoing fiscal year's original budget. That allocation was later revised to Rs 11.75 billion.Major military imports and defence acquisitions are generally funded outside the main defence services allocation and remain undisclosed.The US state department's assessment therefore highlights a distinction between Pakistan's publicly disclosed defence allocation and the wider military spending that may not be fully visible through the country's budgetary documents.The state department's recommendations focus on bringing military and intelligence expenditure into the broader framework of public financial oversight.While the report recognised that Pakistan publishes key budget documents, it identified defence and intelligence spending, debt disclosure and the timing of budget publication as areas requiring greater transparency.The recommendations would require Pakistan to give lawmakers and the public greater visibility into military and intelligence allocations, as well as government liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises.
Article Summary: US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency. Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion for 2026-27 financial year. US state department flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending. Report also raised concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing executive budget proposal.

Article Title: PML-N set to form 'government' in PoK after two former 'premiers' lose strongholds in third phase
Article Text:
Two former PoK premiers lost their strongholds in the third phase of elections marred by violence and rigging allegations, as the PML-N emerged dominant

Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections, according to unofficial results released on Tuesday, while incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat.The latest results came after voting in four constituencies on Monday, with the election process again overshadowed by violence and allegations of rigging. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation and is expected to be held on August 21, according to the region's election commission.The PPP won two of the four seats contested in the third phase, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party won one each. The latter is backed by both Jamaat-e-Islami and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).Former prime minister and Muslim Conference president Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, who was backed by the PML-N, lost the seat in Western Bagh's Dhirkot constituency to Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sardar Sajid Iqbal, according to unofficial results. The seat had been held by the Muslim Conference/PML-N since 1985.In Central Bagh, PPP's Zia Qamar retained the seat, defeating PML-N candidate Mushtaq Minhas.Former premier Sardar Tanveer Ilyas, who joined the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party, secured only a few thousand votes.The result in Eastern Bagh remained pending after authorities ordered a re-poll at 12 polling stations. PML-N candidate Sardar Mir Akbar was leading based on results from 174 of the constituency's 186 polling stations, followed by PPP candidate Sardar Qamaruz Zaman Khan.The election comes against the backdrop of a striking shift in the Pakistani government's treatment of the protest movement that has rocked PoK for months.Just days before the final phase of voting, Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif had described the protesters as "enemies of Pakistan" and ruled out talks with them. But Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's adviser Rana Sanaullah subsequently said 99% of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) were "patriotic brothers", promising that a PML-N government would engage with the group and seek to resolve its demands.The reversal in rhetoric came as the PML-N emerged as the dominant force in the election and prepared to form the next government in the region. The party has secured 25 of the 45 directly elected seats so far, while the PPP has won 12 and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party one.The first two phases, held on July 27 and August 2, were also marked by violent protests and allegations of widespread rigging, with the PML-N and PPP accusing each other of electoral malpractice. Supporters of the two parties clashed at several polling stations.The JAAC has been protesting across the region since early June, with demands including the abolition of 12 refugee seats that it says can be used to influence the formation of governments in PoK.The group has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during violence surrounding the first phase of voting and that around 400 protesters had been killed since the protests began. The Pakistani government has rejected the higher figure as exaggerated, while Sanaullah has acknowledged that deaths from the unrest were in the "double figures".India does not recognise Pakistan's control over the territory, maintaining that Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable parts of India and describing Pakistan's presence in areas under its control as "illegal and forcible occupation".
Article Summary: Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections. Incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation.

Article Title: 'Discontent answered with bullets': MEA slams Pakistan over PoK crackdown

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday slammed Pakistan for its ongoing crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, calling upon the international community to hold the country accountable for the "gross violation of human rights. Polling started in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts at 8 am, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.Clashes between Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) workers were reported in some areas as the region's election commission classified most of the 803 polling stations as "sensitive or highly sensitive".After the first and second phases of polling, which were marred by violent protests and were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively, voting was scheduled for Monday in 11 constituencies of the Poonch Division in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Article Title: After weeks of violent protests, PoK votes in final election phase amid PTI, JAAC boycott calls

Article Title: From 'enemies' to 'patriotic brothers': Pakistan changes stance on PoK protesters ahead of polls
Article Text:
Pakistan PML-N has softened its stance on PoK protesters, calling them "patriotic brothers", as the party prepares to form a government in the region.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s led PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), with a senior government adviser now describing the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” and saying the party will soon engage with them.Sharif’s adviser Rana Sanaullah on Saturday said 99 per cent of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the group leading months of protests in the region, were “our patriotic brothers”.“When the PML(N) government will be formed with two-third majority, it will sit with [Joint Awami] Action Committee representatives. Their first task will be to resolve this issue,” Sanaullah said at a rally ahead of the third and final phase of elections in PoK.The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.Just days earlier, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif had likened the protesters to India and described them as “enemies of Pakistan”, ruling out talks with them. Asif had said there would be “no dialogue with the protesters” and that he considered them in the same category as India.India, however, has rejected Pakistan's stance on the unrest, saying the protests are a direct consequence of Pakistan's economic exploitation, denial of fundamental rights and administrative oppression in PoK.Sanaullah had also previously accused the protesters of seeking to seize Muzaffarabad and Mirpur by force and described their actions as an “India-like attack”. The government had disputed claims of civilian deaths during clashes and accused protesters of opening fire at security personnel.The JAAC, however, has alleged that security forces opened fire on its activists during protests and long marches, with the group claiming that more than 40 people, including women and children, had been killed since elections began and around 400 protesters had been killed since early June.The Pakistan government has rejected the JAAC's figures as “overly exaggerated”, though Sanaullah has acknowledged that the number of people killed in the protests was in the “two digits” and that security personnel had also died.The change in tone comes as the PML-N prepares to take charge of the so-called government in PoK following elections that have been accompanied by violence and allegations of rigging.In the first two phases of voting, the PML-N has won 25 of the 45 directly elected seats, crossing the majority mark in the so-called legislative assembly. The party is in a direct contest with the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), its coalition partner in Pakistan's federal government.The third and final phase of polling for four seats is scheduled for Monday, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.The JAAC has been leading protests in PoK since June, drawing support from students, traders, transporters, lawyers and social workers. The regional government banned the group in June.The protests have faced a security crackdown, with Amnesty International and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan raising concerns over reports of violence and calling for investigations.The situation also drew concern from the United Nations, when it called for accountability for actions against people engaged in peaceful protest.The United States has also urged Pakistan to exercise restraint amid the unrest, calling on authorities to respect fundamental freedoms and create conditions for free and fair elections.
Article Summary: Pakistan PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) A senior government adviser has now described the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.

Article Title: 'Shouldn't be exclusive club': Pak minister seeks Nato-like Islamic military alliance
Article Text:
"I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said.

A day after Pakistan signed a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif on Saturday called for Islamic countries to set aside their differences and form a military alliance along the lines of Nato.In an interview with Geo News, Asif said the agreement signed in Mecca should not remain an "exclusive club" and should be expanded to include other Islamic countries."See, we can't close the doors for other countries. This shouldn't be an exclusive club. This is my personal opinion. It should expand," Asif said."I think Muslim countries should keep their differences, transactional or bilateral disputes aside, on the lines of Nato and stand together," he added.Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday, marking a significant strategic development in the region. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three, drawing comparisons with Nato's Article 5 collective-defence principle.The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the agreement is "guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states" and their shared strategic interests, defence cooperation and "enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity".The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all, according to a joint statement.The pact comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries face missile attacks and disruptions to energy shipments amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran and its regional allies. The conflict escalated after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional crisis.A Turkish official said the agreement was purely defensive, was not directed at any particular country and remained open to participation by other regional nations. The official added that it would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral security arrangements.
Article Summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three. The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.

Article Title: 'There needs to be accountability': UN warns Pakistan over crackdown on peaceful PoK protesters
Article Text:
Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) draws international attention. (Photo: ANI)

The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access, a spokesperson for UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres said.Asked whether the UN would seek accountability for the reported crackdown on protesters, deputy spokesman for the secretary-general Farhan Haq said authorities must ensure that people are allowed to exercise their right to peaceful protest.“It’s important that all authorities everywhere allow for peaceful protest, and certainly that is the case here. If there have been people harmed for engaging in peaceful protest, there needs to be accountability for that,” Haq told PTI.“The Secretary-General supports the work of his high commissioner, and we certainly hope that the pleas made by Mr Turk will be listened to,” he added.UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations into deaths among both protesters and security personnel.According to the UN, dozens of people, mostly protesters but also members of the law enforcement agencies, had reportedly been killed since June as tensions rose ahead of elections to the legislative assembly.Turk had also called for calm and urged authorities to address the underlying grievances of the local population through meaningful and inclusive political dialogue.The UN human rights chief further criticised Pakistan’s decision to ban the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and arrest some of its leaders.The JAAC, a coalition of traders, transporters, students, lawyers, activists and other groups, has been leading protests over political and economic issues in the region.The UN also raised concerns over restrictions on internet access and public gatherings, warning that such measures could undermine the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.“We urge the authorities to ensure full Internet access throughout the territory,” the UN statement said.The comments from the UN come amid heightened tensions in PoK, where protests and violence have also disrupted the regional election process.The JAAC has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during the first phase of polling on July 27 and has claimed that around 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June. The Pakistan government has rejected the figures as “overly exaggerated”.“The number of people killed in the protests is in two digits. Moreover, security personnel have also lost their lives,” Pakistan Prime Minister’s adviser Rana Sanaullah said in a recent television interview.The unrest has also affected the election process in PoK. Authorities on Friday postponed voting indefinitely in seven of the 11 constituencies scheduled to vote in the third phase on August 10, citing concerns over the law-and-order situation. The first two phases of polling, held on July 27 and August 2, were marred by violent protests and allegations of rigging.
Article Summary: The United Nations has warned Pakistan and called for accountability for any action taken against people participating in peaceful protests. This came amid continuing unrest and concerns over restrictions on public gatherings and internet access. UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk had last month expressed concern over the escalating unrest in PoK.

Article Title: 'Exercise restraint, act according to law': US urges Pakistan amid PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Representative image

United States on Friday urged the Pakistan government to exercise restraint amid its ongoing crackdown on citizens following violent protests.Speaking to news agency ANI, a US state department spokesperson urged Pakistani authorities to create conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted peacefully."As with electoral proceedings around the world, we urge officials to create the conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted in a peaceful manner, including ensuring access to information," the spokesperson said.The state department also called on local authorities to exercise restraint and act in accordance with the country's laws and Constitution."We call on all protesters to express their grievances peacefully, and we call on local authorities to exercise restraint, act in accordance with their country's laws and Constitution, and respect fundamental freedoms as they seek to maintain order," the spokesperson added.The remarks came as at least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats. It has alleged that Pakistan's establishment manipulates these seats to install a prime minister of its choice to lead the so-called PoK government.According to JAAC, more than 40 people were killed during the first phase of polling on July 27. It also claims that around 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June.The Shehbaz Sharif government has rejected the claims, calling the figures "overly exaggerated"."The number of people killed in the protests is in two digits. Moreover, security personnel have also lost their lives," Prime Minister's Adviser Rana Sanaullah said in a recent television interview.Meanwhile, voting in seven of the 11 constituencies scheduled for the third phase of polls in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir on August 10 has been postponed indefinitely due to "concerns over the law-and-order situation", authorities announced on Friday.After the first and second phases of polling, which were marred by violent protests, were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively, voting was scheduled for Monday in 11 constituencies of the Poonch Division in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.There are 53 seats in the so-called PoK Legislative Assembly - 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.The second phase of polling on August 2 was marred by violence and allegations of rigging. One person was killed and several others were injured. The phase also included voting for the 12 refugee seats, which are at the centre of the ongoing controversy.Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) swept the second phase, winning 16 seats, while Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured the remaining five.In the first phase on July 27, PML-N won nine of the 13 seats, while PPP won four. With the first two phases combined, PML-N has already secured 24 seats.
Article Summary: U.S. urges Pakistan to create conditions for free and fair elections that can be conducted peacefully. At least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July. Banned Joint Awami Action Committee has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats.

Article Title: Unknown gunmen kill Pakistani policeman, abduct another in separate incidents
Article Text:
The motive behind both the incidents could not immediately be ascertained.

A police constable was shot dead and another was abducted in two separate attacks in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, officials said on Thursday.The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way.In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam, who served in the Special Branch, was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home to report for duty in Bannu district.According to police, Alam regularly used the same route to reach his workplace. He was attacked near Masoomabad on the Bannu-Miranshah Road within the jurisdiction of Cantt Police Station. The assailants fled immediately after carrying out the shooting.In a separate incident, Constable Irfanullah, a wireless operator posted at Shaheed Mureed Akbar Police Station, was abducted from his native village of Sheikh Awtar in Tank district while he was on leave.District Police Officer, Tank, said a search operation had been launched and an investigation into the abduction was underway, adding that efforts were being made to ensure the safe recovery of the abducted constable.
Article Summary: The incidents took place late on Wednesday night in Bannu and Tank districts. Police said the motive behind the attacks remains unclear and investigations are under way. In the first incident, Constable Noor Alam was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him while he was travelling from his home.

Article Title: Pakistan's crackdown in PoK: How Islamabad is tightening information chokehold amid global scrutiny
Article Text:
Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media (ANI photo)

Pakistan's widening crackdown in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) has drawn international attention, with members of the Kashmiri diaspora, rights groups and global watchdogs raising concerns over restrictions on journalists and media freedom.The measures, introduced by the Shehbaz Sharif government during the so-called assembly elections in the illegally-occupied Valley, have also been criticised by press freedom organisations.According to The New York Times, Pakistan has imposed strict rules requiring journalists working for foreign media outlets to seek government permission before travelling outside Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.The restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where demonstrators have been demanding greater political autonomy since early June.The NYT reported that the restrictions could severely affect independent reporting from Pakistan."Heavy local journalists say will close off one of the last remaining ways to get independent journalism about the world’s fifth-most-populous country," the report said.Pakistan has also ordered journalists working for foreign media organisations to leave PoK immediately."The requirement that journalists obtain state approval to report from large parts of the country sends a chilling message: that critical reporting is unwelcome," Pakistan’s leading human rights organisation said in a statement.Journalists covering developments in PoK have come under particular pressure. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), two independent Pakistani journalists were detained on August 1 and taken to an undisclosed location.Several others have reportedly been summoned to court under a law that criminalises "false and fake information" over their reporting from the region.The new restrictions have also been criticised internationally. Patricia Gossman, Human Rights Watch’s senior associate Asia director, called them an "alarming step in the country’s narrowing space for press freedom and free expression." Pakistan ranks 153rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders Press Freedom Index.The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists also urged the Sharif-led government to withdraw the restrictions. "If the government is really interested in showing that it believes in democracy and press freedom, then it should immediately lift this ban," the organisation said.Pakistan's ministry of information, however, said foreign media organisations would continue to operate normally and that the government was working on a new system for issuing travel permits.The restrictions are expected to have the biggest impact on reporting from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where the election process is scheduled to conclude on August 10.The region has witnessed months of protests demanding constitutional reforms, while authorities accuse protesters of violence and demonstrators accuse security forces of suppressing peaceful protests.According to local officials and independent estimates cited by the NYT, at least 30 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.Meanwhile, India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK. The ministry of external affairs called the local elections as "a complete farce." The MEA also highlighted the situation gripped with violence, blackouts, intimidation, and repression against civilians.The Kashmiri diaspora abroad has also staged a strong demonstration in UK. The agitated people took to the streets of Bradford, condemning Pakistan's crackdown in PoK.
Article Summary: Pakistan imposes strict restrictions on media. Restrictions come amid increased media coverage of protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Kashmiri diaspora abroad has staged a strong demonstration in UK. India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK.

Article Title: Imran Khan's three years in jail spark protests across Pakistan; over 100 held
Article Text:
More than 100 supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested as rallies were held across Pakistan on Wednesday to mark the completion of three years of his imprisonment.

Peshawar rally sets September 27 deadline

Family, PTI leaders raise detention concerns

Over 100 supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan were arrested on Wednesday as Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of his imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security.The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power. The party demanded Khan’s release and restoration of his rights. Thousands of supporters gathered amid heavy security, according to Al Jazeera.In Punjab, Police baton-charged protesters and arresting scores of PTI workers in Lahore, Mianwali and Rawalpindi. In Lahore's Mall Road, police dispersed demonstrators demanding Khan's release and detained several protesters.Video footage circulated on social media showed rapid response force (RRF) using force against demonstrators. Some journalists covering the rally were also allegedly thrashed by police, prompting protests from media bodies.PTI Punjab general secretary Chaudhry Bilal Ejaz said five party lawmakers were among 25 others arrested in Lahore.“Despite this era of oppression, repression, and fascism, a large number of PTI workers and office-bearers in Punjab staged protest rallies and pledged to stand with Imran Khan,” he told news agency PTI.According to PTI, at least 50 workers were arrested in Mianwali, Rawalpindi and other parts of Punjab. In Karachi, police used tear gas to disperse PTI supporters protesting in Saddar Town and arrested more than 10 demonstrators. The party also claimed six workers were arrested in Pano Aqil and 15 in Kandhkot.On Wednesday, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Muhammad Suhail Afridi announced that PTI supporters will march towards Islamabad on September 27 if 'justice' is not provided to Khan.Addressing supporters in Peshawar, Afridi said the party's first demand was for cases against Khan and his wife to be heard and decided on merit. Its second demand, he said, was restoration of meetings with their legal team, doctors, relatives and party leaders.He claimed that if justice is delivered, Khan can be released “within 30 minutes”. Otherwise, he said, people from across Pakistan will march to Islamabad on September 27.Aleema Khan, sister of the ousted PM, said the movement for his release had already begun and its next phase would be announced soon.PTI senior leader Moonis Elahi alleged that Khan “has been denied meetings and proper medical treatment, and his eyesight has also deteriorated” in prison.Khan, 73, was arrested on August 5, 2023, and has remained in prison while facing multiple cases. His party has repeatedly alleged that the cases are politically motivated, a charge denied by the Shehbaz Sharif-led government.Amnesty International, a global non-governmental organization, also called on Pakistani authorities to uphold Khan's rights. Acting Regional Director for South Asia Isabelle Lassee said, “For three years, Pakistan’s authorities have systematically denied Imran Khan the right to a fair trial, subjected him to prolonged solitary confinement, and limited his access to medical care and visitation rights.”Lassee further said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family for more than eight months and that he and his wife, Bushra Bibi, had been denied regular access to legal counsel since December 2025.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of Imran Khan's imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security. The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Peace talks abroad, protests at home: The many contradictions shaping Pakistan today
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir (R) (PTI file photo)

From military confrontation to diplomatic outreach

The Iran gamble

A war next door, and Pakistan's opportunity

Living on lifelines, dreaming of leadership

Source: IMF

Security ambitions amid diplomatic outreach

Diplomacy abroad, discontent within

Operation Sindoor 's lasting fallout

Operation Sindoor fallout

Sites targeted during Op Sindoor

The Balochistan challenge refuses to fade

BLA

Pakistan's uneasy neighbourhood

Presence of TTP remains a major challenge for Pakistan

A nation seeking influence while confronting instability

"A house divided against itself cannot stand." Abraham Lincoln's observation aptly captures Pakistan 's situation.While Islamabad chases the image of an indispensable diplomatic player, its own foundations appear increasingly fragile. From brokering peace in Middle East to courting Washington and Beijing, Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy.Yet back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, water shortages, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses, an uneasy contradiction that defines the country's present-day reality.Much of Pakistan's strategic direction continues to be shaped by its military establishment, with army chief Asim Munir, the country's de facto centre of power. His influence extends well beyond defence matters, as Pakistan's military continues to function as a parallel authority that heavily influences domestic governance as well as foreign policy.That contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.Just over a year ago, Pakistan suffered one of its most difficult periods on the diplomatic and military fronts following India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in South Kashmir's Pahalgam.New Delhi's "zero-tolerance" policy under Prime Minister Narendra Modi translated into a series of retaliatory actions that once again placed Pakistan under international scrutiny over terrorism.Yet, even as tensions with India remained elevated, Islamabad quickly sought to recast its international image.Already maintaining close ties with China, Pakistan simultaneously attempted to deepen engagement with Donald Trump's United States. For a country grappling with a fragile economy, maintaining goodwill with both Washington and Beijing has become increasingly important.It was in this backdrop that Pakistan pitched itself as a potential mediator between Iran and the United States.Pakistan's bid to position itself as a regional peace broker did not begin smoothly.Its initial attempt to host talks between Iran and the United States faltered after Tehran rejected Islamabad as the venue. According to The Wall Street Journal, Iran formally informed mediators that it would not attend the proposed talks with American officials in Pakistan.Islamabad, however, persisted.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and military head Asim Munir stepped up engagement with Washington, with Munir's growing proximity to the Trump administration earning him the title of Trump's "favourite field marshal".Around the same time, Sharif attended President Xi Jinping 's grand military parade in Beijing alongside leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The event reinforced Pakistan's continued strategic closeness with China even as it simultaneously sought stronger engagement with Washington.Six months later, the geopolitical landscape shifted dramatically as President Donald Trump launched military strikes against Iran, joined by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under Operation Epic Fury.Global Shia icon and longest-ruling Supreme Leader of Iran Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the opening day of the offensive on February 28, 2026 in Pakistan's neighbourhood.The raging Tehran regime's response left the Middle East region totally disturbed. Bombs, missiles and drones fell, almost hitting every country in the region.Retaliatory strikes and military activity engulfed large parts of the region, with airspace disrupted across Iraq, Kuwait, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, Oman, Jordan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.However, Pakistan, despite its border with Iran, remained untouched and safe.That made Islamabad a potential venue for talks with Iran's new leadership under Mojtaba Khamenei .Sensing an opportunity, Pakistan declared itself a peace broker. On April 8, Sharif posted on X announcing a ceasefire that actually wasn't close to peace.He wrote: "With the greatest humility, I am pleased to announce that the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States of America, along with their allies, have agreed to an immediate ceasefire everywhere including Lebanon and elsewhere, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY."In May, army chief Asim Munir hailed the development as "slight progress". US Vice President JD Vance visited Pakistan twice for peace talks, but despite the diplomatic efforts, the fighting continued and a lasting peace remained elusive.Still, the symbolism was already disheartening. The same country where the US carried out Operation Neptune Spear to eliminate Osama bin Laden had now become Washington's chosen venue for talks with Iran.Islamabad may be eager to wear the badge of a global player, but its economic reality tells a far less flattering story. Beneath the grand diplomatic posturing lies a cash-strapped nation surviving on lifelines from China, the United States, the IMF and other international lenders, hardly the profile of a country calling the shots on the world stage.According to Reuters, the IMF in May completed reviews of its lending programmes with Pakistan, clearing the way for approximately $1.32 billion in fresh funding.The package included nearly $1.1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and around $220 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, taking total disbursements under the two ongoing programmes to roughly $4.8 billion.Pakistan remains under a $7-billion IMF programme after reaching a staff-level agreement in March."Amid a more challenging and highly uncertain external environment since the onset of the war in the Middle East, Pakistan needs to maintain strong macroeconomic policies while accelerating reform efforts," the IMF said in a statement.For Islamabad, therefore, diplomacy is not merely about regional influence. It is also about preserving the confidence of the international community at a time when its economy remains deeply dependent on external financing.Alongside its mediation efforts, Pakistan has also sought to deepen strategic partnerships within the Islamic world.Islamabad has moved closer to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, readying a Nato-style Islamic security arrangement with mutual defence provisions reminiscent to Nato.The defence pact, signed by Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in September, states that "any aggression" against one member would be treated as an attack on all , a provision that closely mirrors Nato's Article 5. Turkey, already a Nato member, fields the alliance's second-largest military after the United States.While the arrangement remains far from becoming a formal military alliance, it reflects Islamabad's broader effort to strengthen its regional security architecture to counter New Delhi.However, the economic and military size of the two-nuclear armed nations still remain widely different.Pakistan lagging far behind.Even with Islamabad's projected flamboyancy in foreign dealings, unrest continues across Pakistan and regions illegally occupied by Pakistan.The most visible flashpoint in recent months has been Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), where the so-called Assembly elections have been conducted in three phases amid allegations of police excesses and restrictions on dissent.Videos and reports emerging from the region have shown violent confrontations between security forces and protesters, prompting criticism from rights groups and attracting international attention.Pakistan's own defence minister, Khawaja Asif, further fuelled controversy with remarks defending the government's actions."I put the protesters of PoJK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Asif said.The statement reflected Islamabad's increasingly uncompromising approach towards dissent in the region.The ministry of external affairs strongly denounced Pakistan's mischievous handling of the situation, describing the elections in PoK as a "complete farce". The MEA also condemned the Islamabad-backed ill-treatment and crackdown that killed 90 people in the region since June this year.Human rights organisations have echoed similar concerns.Amnesty International USA called reports emerging from PoK's Rawalakot as "disturbing" and urged Pakistani authorities to restore communication services and permit independent media and observers into the region."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The developments have reinforced criticism that, while Islamabad attempts to mediate conflicts abroad, it continues to face accusations of suppressing dissent within territories under its own control.Behind the fancy overcoat of its foreign policy ambitions, Pakistan ultimately bore the brunt of its fertile terror fields it had long nurtured.The fallout from Operation Sindoor did not just damage Pakistan-backed terror camps and military infrastructure.India swiftly showcased the scale of its response, striking nine terror bases and 11 military installations across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).The consequences of Operation Sindoor extended beyond military targets to the country's most basic necessities, including water. With all major rivers in Pakistan flowing into its territory from India, New Delhi had placed the decades-old Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance immediately after the Pahalgam massacre of April 22, 2025.The country is facing an increasingly severe water crisis, particularly across Sindh and Balochistan , where shrinking river flows and uneven distribution have triggered alarm among farmers, political leaders and water experts.Months after New Delhi's decision, Pakistan is confronting growing concerns over agricultural losses, declining livelihoods and mounting economic pressure across several provinces.Sindh, home to Karachi, Pakistan's financial capital, has emerged as one of the worst-hit regions, with water shortages threatening agriculture and affecting millions of people.Prime Minister Narendra Modi had encapsulated India's position soon after the Pahalgam attack."Terror and talks cannot go together; water and blood cannot flow together," he had said.The message was reiterated recently by defence minister Rajnath Singh recently on Kargil Vijay Diwas."After the Pahalgam terror attack, by suspending the Indus Waters Treaty, we said that those whose tears have dried up should not expect water from us. We will not let the waters of the Sindhu reach the patrons of terrorists and enemies of humanity," Rajnath said.For Pakistan, the water crisis has added yet another layer to an already fragile economic and political situation, with experts warning that prolonged shortages could further aggravate regional discontent.While PoK has dominated headlines in recent weeks, Balochistan continues to represent Pakistan's longest-running internal security challenge.The province recently announced plans to observe its own Independence Day, underlining the persistence of separatist sentiment.The conflict, rooted in grievances dating back to Balochistan's accession to Pakistan in 1948, revolves around demands for greater political autonomy, control over natural resources and opposition to mega infrastructure projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).Over the decades, the conflict has been marked by armed insurgency, heavy militarisation and repeated allegations of human rights violations.Yet Balochistan is only one strand of Pakistan's broader internal unrest.The country's dissent is neither unified nor driven by a single cause.Separatist groups in Balochistan, the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, political activists and unemployed youth often pursue vastly different objectives.That fragmentation, however, has also worked to the advantage of Pakistan's establishment.Without a unified opposition, the state has been able to confront each movement differently, labelling one as terrorism, another as separatism, others as political disorder or foreign conspiracy.Rather than confronting a single nationwide challenge, Islamabad faces multiple disconnected crises, each requiring a different response.For neighbouring Iran, Pakistan has recently struck the chord of "peace", offering itself as a mediator, though the negotiations have yielded almost no progress.Its ties with Tehran, however, have rarely been straightforward. Relations with India remain frozen, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi making New Delhi's position unequivocal: "If there will be talks between India and Pakistan, it will only be on terrorism and PoK."To the west, Pakistan's troubles are no less daunting. Crossborder tensions with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan have intensified, even as Islamabad grapples with a surge in terror attacks at home.Beyond the long-running insurgency in Balochistan, Pakistan faces an increasingly potent threat from the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). While the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, Islamabad's hopes of gaining strategic leverage quickly unraveled. Kabul has refused to dismantle TTP sanctuaries, allowing the outfit to regroup and intensify attacks across Pakistan.The fallout has been severe. Cross-border clashes have become more frequent, while the TTP, an umbrella militant group formed in 2007, continues to challenge the Pakistani state's authority, specifying the irony of a country seeking to broker peace abroad while battling an escalating insurgency at home.Pakistan today finds itself pursuing two parallel realities.On one hand, it is attempting to establish itself as a regional diplomatic player, offering to mediate conflicts, expanding defence partnerships and seeking greater geopolitical relevance.On the other, it continues to wrestle with economic fragility, dependence on IMF assistance, unrest in PoK and Balochistan, a worsening water crisis and an increasingly complex internal security landscape.Adding to these challenges is the country's continued struggle with terrorism. According to the Global Terrorism Index 2026, Pakistan ranked as the country most affected by terrorism, recording more than 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.For Islamabad, diplomatic visibility on the global stage may offer strategic dividends and international goodwill. But as long as domestic crises continue to deepen, Pakistan's ambitions abroad will remain overshadowed by the challenges it faces at home.
Article Summary: Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy. But back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses. The contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.

Article Title: Bangladesh PM likely to visit India as Dhaka presses for Sheikh Hasina's extradition
Article Text:
Tarique Rahman likely to visit India

Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed visit to India has not yet been finalised, with the timing dependent on his “schedule” and the “progress” of ongoing bilateral discussions."The government is positive about visits to all countries. But it will depend on the PM's schedule and on how far discussions between the two countries progress," state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam said."The government is busy, and so is the prime minister. If everything fits together, of course there will be a visit to India, a visit to Japan; all the visits will happen," she said, referring to ongoing domestic programmes and upcoming constitutional activities.In April, Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman visited India as part of efforts to mend strained bilateral ties following more than 18 months of heightened diplomatic tensions.Bangladesh has also sought the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Tuesday that India has extended two separate invitations to Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman — one for a bilateral visit and another to attend the outreach session of the Brics Summit in New Delhi in September."Brics is still a long way off. A lot can happen in a month,” Shama said.Asked whether Rahman’s visit to India could help ease tensions, Shama said direct communication between the leaders of the two governments could provide an opportunity to discuss and resolve outstanding issues."Whenever the heads of two countries talk, there is a chance of resolving many problems. That opportunity is there; it remains," she said.Relations between India and Bangladesh deteriorated sharply after the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus came to power following the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government in August 2024.Efforts to stabilise ties gained momentum after Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, accompanied by foreign secretary Vikram Misri, represented India at Tarique Rahman’s swearing-in ceremony in Dhaka on February 17.Rahman assumed office as prime minister after his party secured a landslide victory in the parliamentary elections.Bangladesh’s current government, led by Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party, has maintained that Sheikh Hasina must surrender and face the law if she returns to the country.Hasina recently addressed an audio-only virtual press conference from New Delhi, her first public media interaction since fleeing to India on August 5, 2024, amid mass protests.During the virtual press conference, Hasina said she was determined to return to Bangladesh in December to put the country on the "right track" by restoring democracy, despite facing the possibility of imprisonment or a death sentence.India distanced itself from Hasina’s media interaction, clarifying that it had neither played a role in organising the event nor endorsed her remarks concerning the Bangladesh government.
